sens: Man of the tribe of Issachar
Son of Thola
Chief of a paternal house
H3400.detail: Jériel is a man belonging to the tribe of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He is the son of Thola and is part of a brotherhood of six brothers — Uzzi, Rephaja, Jachmaï, Jibsam, and Samuel — all chiefs of paternal houses, meaning they are responsible for extended families within their clan. These six men are among the valiant warriors of David's generation: at the time of the Davidic census, the total number of warriors from Thola amounts to twenty-two thousand six hundred (1 Chronicles 7:2), demonstrating the importance and strength of this branch of Issachar. Jériel thus represents a figure of local and military authority within his people.
H3400.origine: The name literally means "taught of God" or "God teaches," combining the divine name (El) with an element evoking divine instruction. It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, expressing the relationship between the bearer and God. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, but each is a distinct individual.
H3400.emploi: Jériel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:2, in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar during the time of David. He is presented solely by his family status — son of Thola, brother of five other chiefs — and his administrative and military role. His appearance is brief and purely genealogical, without a specific account of his actions.

sens: one who opposes someone, who fights or threatens them
the enemy in an armed or political conflict
one who contests the rights or cause of someone
H3401.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who directly opposes a person, either through hostility or contestation. It is a rival, a competitor who seeks to harm or defeat. In Psalms 35:1, the psalmist asks God to "defend him against his adversaries": these are those who fight against him, who harbor ill will toward him.
2. It can designate the enemy in a military or political sense, one who makes war or exercises oppression. In Isaiah 49:25, the Lord promises to "fight the enemies" of His people and to save them: these are the hostile powers that threaten Israel.
3. The word can also evoke one who contests or accuses, who raises a complaint against someone. In Jeremiah 18:19, the prophet asks God to hear the voice of his "adversaries": these are those who oppose him, who slander him, or who wish to destroy him.
H3401.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "contesting" or "disputing." It is built on the same base as the verb "rib" (to contend, to enter into litigation), which expresses the action of confronting someone, quarreling with them, or pleading one's case against them. It is thus a word that speaks of conflict, active opposition, not mere passive disagreement.
H3401.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided usages: in Psalms 35:1 (adversaries), in Isaiah 49:25 (enemies), and in Jeremiah 18:19 (adversaries). The Segond translates it either as "adversary" (Psalms and Jeremiah) or as "enemy" (Isaiah). In all cases, it designates one who opposes with hostility: personal enemies who harass the psalmist, the powers that threaten God's people, or those who slander the prophet. The biblical context always emphasizes active and often violent opposition.
H3401.portee: This word reminds us that the believer's life is not free from conflicts and opposition. The Bible does not deny the existence of adversaries; rather, it teaches that it is God who intervenes to defend His people and His servants. Calling upon the Lord against adversaries is to recognize that true strength lies not in our ability to fight, but in the protection and justice of God.

sens: Man of the exile and return period, mentioned only once in the Bible
H3402G.detail: Jarib is a proper name designating a man living at the time of the return from exile (around the 5th century BCE). The Bible mentions him only once, in Ezra 8:16, where he is listed among the leaders of Israel whom the prophet Ezra summons for an important mission.
H3402G.origine: The name Jarib literally means "he contends" or "he defends," deriving from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of pleading a case or opposing. This name reveals the character or authority of the bearer: someone capable of defending their position, like many Hebrew names that reflect a quality or expected action of the bearer.
H3402G.emploi: Jarib appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:16. He is presented as one of the leaders that Ezra gathers before leaving Babylon to return to Jerusalem. In this context, he represents one of the civil or religious authorities tasked with contributing to the return of the exiles and the restoration of life in Israel. His name appears in a list of important figures of the time, indicating his status and role in the restored community.

sens: priest son of Jozadak at the time of the return from exile
H3402H.detail: Jarib is a priest, son of Jozadak and brother of Joshua, who returns from exile in Babylon with Ezra. He is among the priests who married foreign women, which was prohibited by the Law (Ezra 10:18).
H3402H.origine: The name Jarib literally means "he contends" or "he disputes" in Hebrew, formed from the root of contention or combat. It is a name that evokes the ability to plead or oppose. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, but this one is specifically known as a priest at the time of the return from exile.
H3402H.emploi: Jarib appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:18, in the list of priests who had to send away their foreign wives after returning from Babylon. He is mentioned alongside his brothers Maaséja, Eliezer, and Gedaliah, all sons of Joshua and Jozadak. This moment is crucial: it marks the purification of the priesthood and the restoration of the boundaries of the covenant after the exile.

sens: son of Simeon
warrior or one who contends
H3402I.detail: 1. Jarib is a son of Simeon, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:24 among the sons of this patriarch. The same character appears in Genesis 46:10 under another name, Jachin, which shows that the same individual could bear two names in biblical genealogies.
H3402I.origine: The name Jarib comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to contend" or "to dispute." This root evokes the idea of one who defends their cause or enters into conflict. The name thus carries a nuance of combativeness or strength of character. It is a name from the tribe of Simeon, and it also appears as another name for Jachin.
H3402I.emploi: Jarib is mentioned only once in the preserved biblical usages, in 1 Chronicles 4:24, where he appears in the genealogical list of the sons of Simeon. He is a character from the time of Egypt and the desert. The genealogical context shows that this name served to identify descendants and preserve the memory of the families of the people of Israel.

sens: Warrior in the service of King David
H3403.detail: Jeribaï is a man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:46, where he is listed among the "mighty men" (or high-ranking warriors) who fought alongside King David.
H3403.origine: The name Jeribaï literally means "my contentions" or "my disputes," formed from the Hebrew root of the verb "to contend," "to dispute." It is a theophoric name, meaning it implicitly contains a reference to God (the suffix "-i" can refer to a personal relationship with the divine). Jeribaï is the son of Elnaam and the brother of Joschavia, both mentioned in the lists of David's mighty warriors.
H3403.emploi: Jeribaï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:46. He is cited in a list of elite warriors that David gathered around him to strengthen his army. This list enumerates men of valor, some from the region of Machavim. Jeribaï is presented as a prestigious warrior, worthy of being mentioned alongside the mighty men who supported David. No additional details about his life or exploits are provided by the biblical text.
H3403.portee: Jeribaï reminds the reader that King David's reign was built on the dedication of faithful and courageous warriors. His name, which means "my contentions," may evoke the struggles and battles that marked Israel's history. This character also illustrates the importance that the Bible places on faithfulness and courage alongside those whom God calls to serve.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Judah, son of Hebron
Chief of the house of Hebron during the organization of the temple service by David
H3404G.detail:
1. Jerija is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi, whose main role was to serve in the temple. He is the son of Hebron and has three brothers: Amariah, Jachaziel, and Jekameam (1 Chronicles 23:19).
2. Jerija is designated as the chief of the house of Hebron at the time when King David organizes and distributes the religious service of the temple among the different families of Levites. This is a position of responsibility among the servants of the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 23:19 and 24:23).
H3404G.origine: The name Jerija means "taught by the Lord" or "that the Lord has taught." It is composed of Hebrew elements expressing the idea of instruction or teaching received from God Himself. This name reflects the belief that a child of God receives wisdom and direction from the Lord.
H3404G.emploi: Jerija appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the first book of Chronicles, in chapters 23 and 24. These two passages are parallel and recount the same event: David's organization of the families of Levites for the service of the temple. Jerija is listed each time as the first and chief of the descendants of Hebron among the Levites. His importance lies in this role as head of a Levitical division during the establishment of public worship in Israel.

sens: Levitical chief of the house of Hebron during the reign of David
H3404H.detail: Jerija was a Levite from the Kohathite family, responsible for leading the group of Hebronites—a branch of the Levites in charge of temple service. During the reign of King David, in an administrative organization of these religious services (in the fortieth year of his reign), genealogical research was conducted to identify capable men within these Levitical families. Jerija was recognized as the head of his house, meaning he was the leader of this important branch of the servants of worship (1 Chronicles 26:31).
H3404H.origine: The name Jerija comes from Hebrew and literally means "taught by the Lord" (from yireh, what is seen or taught, and Yah, the Name of God). It is a theophoric name, composed of the divine name, which expresses trust in divine teaching or guidance. This type of name was common in Levitical families, emphasizing that religious service came from divine instruction.
H3404H.emploi: Jerija appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:31. The context shows that he was an important administrative figure in the organization of worship under David: responsible for an entire Levitical branch, he was notable enough to be mentioned by name during a royal genealogical inquiry. His role reflects the hierarchical structure of Levitical service during the time of the Davidic monarchy.
H3404H.portee: Jerija reminds us that the service of God in the Old Testament was organized and hierarchical, confined to specific families and responsible leaders. His example shows how worship was not improvised but structured according to an order that God Himself had established, with men ensuring its faithful administration.

sens: Canaanite city located west of the Jordan, first stronghold conquered by Israel
Geographical landmark and gathering place for the Israelites
Administrative center and residence of prophets
Symbol of divine promise and victory through faith
H3405G.detail:
1. Jericho is a city located in the Jordan Valley, about 8 kilometers west of the river and 11 kilometers north of the Dead Sea. It is the first city that the Israelites conquer upon entering the Promised Land, according to the account in the book of Joshua. The walls of the city miraculously collapse at the sound of trumpets, giving Jericho a unique place in biblical history (Joshua 6:1-2).
2. The city serves as a landmark for delineating the lands and borders of the tribes of Israel. It is mentioned in descriptions of territorial inheritances and in enumerations of cities (Joshua 16:7, Joshua 18:21).
3. Jericho becomes a center of religious and prophetic life. Prophets reside there, including Elisha, who is surrounded by young prophets; it is near this city that miraculous circumstances unfold (2 Kings 2:4-5, 2 Kings 2:15).
4. The conquest of Jericho embodies the power of God and the trust that Israel must place in Him rather than in its own military strength. This foundational victory will permanently mark the people as an act of divine grace.
H3405G.origine: The Hebrew name יְרִיחוֹ (Jericho) literally means "its moon." This etymology possibly suggests a connection to lunar cults of Canaan or a poetic description of the place. The name has remained unchanged in Greek (Ἱεριχώ) and in French, as it is a proper name established since antiquity. Archaeologically, the city is one of the oldest in the Levant, corresponding to its role in the early accounts of conquest.
H3405G.emploi: Jericho appears 52 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Numbers and Joshua, which recount Israel's arrival in the Promised Land. It first appears in the stages of the desert (Numbers 22:1, Numbers 33:48-50), then becomes the scene of the actual conquest (Joshua 2 to 6). After the city's capture, Jericho is mentioned as a territorial landmark (Joshua 16:7, Joshua 18:21) and as an administrative center. It also appears in the accounts of the kings of Israel and Judah, particularly during the miraculous events of Elisha's cycle (2 Kings 2). The name remains a symbol of Israel's first victory in the Promised Land.
H3405G.portee: Jericho reminds the believer that true victory does not belong to military strength, but to trust in God and obedience to His commands, even when they seem strange or impossible to carry out. The miraculous collapse of its walls demonstrates that God can bring down the most formidable obstacles to establish His people in the inheritance He has promised. For the New Testament disciple, Jericho also evokes a place where encounters of grace arise: that of the tax collector Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1-10) and that of the blind beggar (Luke 18:35-43) who confess Jesus as Lord.

sens: fortified city of Canaan, the first conquered by the Israelites upon their entry into the Promised Land
H3405H.detail: 1. Jericho is the fortified city that God miraculously causes to fall before Joshua and the Israelites at the time of their entry into Canaan — this is the fulfillment of the promise made to Abraham. The name means "its moon" in Hebrew, possibly evoking an ancient lunar sanctuary or simply a significant milestone in the journey. Located 8 kilometers west of the Jordan and near the Dead Sea, in a fertile valley surrounded by palm trees, it occupied a strategic position at the gateway to the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 34:3).
H3405H.origine: The Hebrew name יְרִיחוֹ (Jericho) literally means "its moon" — whether this etymology comes from ירח (yerah, "moon") or from a root denoting freshness (related to the moisture of the oasis) is debated, but the image is that of a prosperous oasis, a lunar refuge in the heart of the desert. The city, which the Bible mainly discusses during the conquest under Joshua, carries symbolic weight: it is the first obstacle, the first public miracle of the entry into Canaan.
H3405H.emploi: The name appears primarily in the accounts of the conquest (book of Joshua) and in later geographical references. In Deuteronomy 34:3, it specifically designates the fertile oasis "the city of palms," visible from the mountain where Moses gazes upon the Promised Land before his death. Jericho embodies the transition from slavery to freedom, from desert to abundance, from struggle to possession.
H3405H.portee: Jericho reminds us that God keeps His promises and acts extraordinarily for His people — its walls fall not by military might, but by faith in God. This victory marks the concrete beginning of the promised inheritance and invites the reader to see God as the true conqueror and protector.

sens: Benjamite, son of Bela
H3406G.detail: Jerimoth is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela and head of a family house. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:7 among the sons of Bela, listed as one of the valiant leaders of this paternal house and recorded in the genealogies with his brothers Etsbon, Uzzi, Uziel, and Iri.
H3406G.origine: The name Jerimoth means "God is very high" or "the Lord is exalted." It is a theophoric name, expressing confidence in divine sovereignty. Although the name is borne by several men in the Old Testament (notably a Levite and other figures), we describe here the Benjamite son of Bela mentioned alone in 1 Chronicles 7:7.
H3406G.emploi: Jerimoth appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:7, in the passage that lists the descendants of Benjamin and their houses. He is presented as one of the five sons of Bela, all heads of family houses and reputed as valiant men. This genealogical passage shows that Jerimoth was a significant figure in the structuring of the tribe of Benjamin in ancient times, probably during the time of Egypt and the desert according to the source.

sens: Benjamite, son of Beker
H3406H.detail: Jerémoth is a man of the people of Israel, from the tribe of Benjamin. He is the son of Beker and appears in the genealogy of the families of Benjamin during the time when Israel was established in Egypt and the desert (1 Chronicles 7:8). Like his brothers, he is mentioned to identify a particular Benjaminite house or lineage, according to the custom of biblical genealogical lists.
H3406H.origine: The name Jerémoth (or Jerimoth) means "He is Most High" or "He is Exalted," likely composed of elements expressing divine greatness. This name was borne by several men in Israel's history, but this one is clearly identified by his genealogy: son of Beker and brother of Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, and others.
H3406H.emploi: Jerémoth appears only once in the provided texts, in 1 Chronicles 7:8, where he is listed among the sons of Beker, a head of a Benjaminite house. This mention fits into the context of the genealogies of the tribes of Israel, which establish the family lineages of each people. It allows for the identification of descendants and the leaders of the various families of the chosen people.

sens: Benjamite, son of Beriah
Head of a house in the genealogy of Benjamin
H3406I.detail:
1. Jérémoth is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Beriah and grandson of Elpahal, living at the time of the formation of the people of Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:14, among the descendants of Benjamin listed in the genealogy of this tribe.
2. He is presented as the head of a house, meaning he led a family or clan within his tribe. This role of head of a house was important in the social organization of Israel: it provided a role and responsibility in managing the family and community affairs of Benjamin.
H3406I.origine: The name Jérémoth (in Hebrew יְרֵמוֹת) literally means "He is the Most High" or "Supreme Elevation," composed of roots evoking height and divine supremacy. This name reflects a confession of faith in the greatness of God. In the Old Testament, several people bear this name or close variants (Jerimouth, Jerémoth), indicating that it was a favored name in Israelite families, particularly among the Benjamites.
H3406I.emploi: Jérémoth appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 8:14. He is included in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, drafted to establish genealogical records after the return from exile. This genealogical list aimed to officially recognize families and their land rights. Although Jérémoth is mentioned briefly, his presence in this record shows that he held a recognized position in the tribal structure of Benjamin. His cited brothers (Arad, Ahio, Shashak, Zebadiah, Eder, Michael, Ishpha, and Joha) indicate that his family was of some importance.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
H3406J.detail: Jerimoth is a name borne by several men in the history of Israel during the time of the divided monarchy. In the unique mention in the Segond at 1 Chronicles 12:5, Jerimoth is among the Benjamites who joined David in the desert when he was fleeing from King Saul. The name appears in a list of valiant warriors who came to strengthen David's troops.
H3406J.origine: The name Jerimoth means "He is the Most High": it combines a form of the verb "to elevate" or "to exalt" with the divine name. It is a theophoric name — a name that contains a statement about God — common in Israel to express confidence in the height and sovereignty of God. The same name was borne by at least eleven different men during the periods of the monarchy and exile, including Benjamites, Levites, and even a son of King David.
H3406J.emploi: Jerimoth appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, always as a personal name. The majority of the Jerimoth mentioned are Benjamites or Levites. In 1 Chronicles 12:5, Jerimoth is cited as one of the warriors who came to strengthen David in the desert, showing that he was a capable and loyal warrior. Other mentions designate him as head of a house, temple musician, royal official, or man married to a foreigner during the time of Ezra, attesting that the name was borne by men of varied ranks throughout Israel's history.

sens: Son of the Levite Mushi, serving in the temple during the royal period of Israel
H3406K.detail: Jerimoth is a Levite from the family of Merari, son of Mushi. He is mentioned in the census of the Levites established by King David for the organization of temple service. The name appears twice in the same genealogies: in 1 Chronicles 23:23 and 24:30, where he is counted among the direct descendants of Mushi, alongside his brothers Machli and Eder. These lists show the importance that the Bible places on the genealogy of the servants of the sanctuary and the transmission of cultic service from generation to generation within Levitical families.
H3406K.origine: The name means "He is the Most High" or "Elevation." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing height or exaltation, combined with the name of God. This man shares the same name as several other biblical characters (some Benjamites, a temple musician under David, an officer under David), indicating that this name was borne by various families in Israel, with no direct kinship between these namesakes.
H3406K.emploi: Jerimoth appears twice in Chronicles, always in genealogical lists of the Levites established under King David. The two occurrences (1 Chronicles 23:23 and 24:30) describe the same person, as they enumerate the sons of Mushi in the same order and context of organizing worship at the temple. These texts do not recount anything particular about him: he is simply recorded as a Levite from the branch of Merari, classified in the official genealogies of divine service in Jerusalem.

sens: Levite son of Heman, temple musician during the time of David
Chief of the fifteenth division of musicians in the service of worship
H3406L.detail:
1. Jérimoth is a Levite, son of the famous musician Heman, mentioned among the twelve musician sons of Heman in 1 Chronicles 25:4. He represents one of the branches of the Levitical musical family that served in the temple.
2. He is designated as chief of the fifteenth division of musicians (1 Chronicles 25:22), with his sons and brothers forming a team of twelve responsible for the cultic musical service. Each division represented an organized group to ensure the continuous service of the temple.
H3406L.origine: The name Jérimoth means "He is the Most High" or "height of God." It is a theophoric name composed to express trust in divine majesty. The name was borne by several people during the divided monarchy, particularly among the families of Benjamites and Levites.
H3406L.emploi: Jérimoth appears twice in 1 Chronicles 25, at the heart of the passage describing the organization of temple musicians under David. The text first lists Jérimoth among the twelve sons of his father Heman (verse 4), then specifically identifies him as responsible for the fifteenth division of musicians (verse 22). This organized system of musical divisions reflects the administrative structure of worship in Jerusalem. Jérimoth represents one of the generations of Levites who continued the musical service of the temple as a family heritage.

sens: Son of Azriel, administrative chief of the tribe of Naphtali under King David
H3406M.detail: Jérimoth is a royal officer appointed to govern the tribe of Naphtali during the reign of King David. He appears in the register of officials that David had placed at the head of each of the twelve tribes of Israel. His role was to oversee the civil and administrative affairs of his region, indicating that he was a trusted man of the king.
H3406M.origine: The name Jérimoth (or Jérimòth) means "He is very high" or "The Most High," combining a Hebrew root expressing elevation or height. It was a name borne by several important figures during the Divided Kingdom: some were Benjamites, others were Levitical musicians, and one was even a son of King David. The repetition of the name suggests that it was a respected name in the official and religious circles of Israel.
H3406M.emploi: This specific man, Jérimoth son of Azriel, appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:19. He is listed among the complete list of twelve tribal leaders that King David had instituted to administer the twelve tribes of Israel in times of peace. This list shows the centralized administrative organization that David had established to govern his kingdom. Several other Jérimoth are mentioned elsewhere in Chronicles, but this specific verse concerns the governor of Naphtali.

sens: Son of David and father of Mahalath, wife of Rehoboam
H3406N.detail: Jérimoth is one of the sons of King David, mentioned only once in the Bible in 2 Chronicles 11:18. He is known because he is the father of Mahalath, who became the wife of King Rehoboam. This marital alliance thus links the descendants of David to those of Rehoboam, strengthening the family ties between two generations of kings of Israel.
H3406N.origine: The name Jérimoth means "He is the Most High" or "The Most High." He bears the name of the God of Israel, like many Hebrew names of that time. The same name was borne by several other biblical characters (notably some Benjamites and Levites), but this one is uniquely identifiable by his genealogy: son of David.
H3406N.emploi: Jérimoth appears only once in the canonical biblical texts, in 2 Chronicles 11:18. He is presented as one of the many sons of King David and as the father of Mahalath. His role is purely genealogical: to establish the kinship between David, his daughter Mahalath, and King Rehoboam who married her. This mention fits into the context of the strategic marriages of the Davidic royalty.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy of Israel
H3406O.detail: Jerimoth is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, at various times. The one mentioned in 2 Chronicles 31:13 was a Levite employed during the reign of King Hezekiah, tasked with managing the contributions and gifts of the temple along with other administrators, under the supervision of Conaniah and Azariah.
H3406O.origine: The name Jerimoth means "He is the Most High" or "Exalted of the Lord," composed of Hebrew elements expressing height and divine exaltation. It is a theophoric name, bearing the name of God, common among Levites and men of high rank in the religious and civil hierarchy of Israel.
H3406O.emploi: Jerimoth is a personal name borne by at least eleven different men in the Old Testament, during the time of the Israelite monarchy. The only attested use in common French translations is that of 2 Chronicles 31:13, where Jerimoth appears as a Levite from the time of King Hezekiah (around the 7th century B.C.), tasked with overseeing and managing the goods dedicated to the temple, indicating a position of trust and responsibility in the administration of worship.

sens: Man who lived during the Exile and Return
H3406P.detail: Jerémoth is the name of a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:26. He was among the men who had married foreign women during the Exile in Babylon and who, at the order of the scribe Ezra, had to repudiate these women to return to faithfulness to the law. This Jerémoth, son of Elam, represents one of those cases of mixed marriage that the people returned from Captivity had to correct.
H3406P.origine: The name Jerémoth (Hebrew יְרֵמוֹת) means "He is the Most High" or "Height of the Lord," composed of Hebrew roots evoking elevation and the divine. Several men bore this name in the history of Israel, notably among the Benjamites and the Levites.
H3406P.emploi: Jerémoth is cited only once in the canonical biblical books, in Ezra 10:26. He appears in the list of the sons of Elam who had contracted marriages with foreign women and who agreed to repudiate them during the religious reform led by Ezra after the return from Babylon. This context highlights the central issue of this period: the reconstitution of Israel around the purity of race and fidelity to the Law.

sens: Israelite man living during the time of exile and return
Several characters bearing this name in the Old Testament
H3406Q.detail:
1. Jerémoth is a proper name borne by several men in the history of Israel. During the time of exile and the return to Jerusalem, the name Jerémoth specifically refers to a man mentioned in Ezra 10:27, who was the son of Zattu and had taken a foreign wife.

2. The name Jerémoth also appears elsewhere in the Old Testament to designate other characters: Benjamites from different generations, a Levite musician of the temple, a military officer in the service of King David, and others. Each Jerémoth is a distinct character with his own lineage and role.
H3406Q.origine: The name Jerémoth (or Jérimoth) means in Hebrew "He is the Most High" or "Height of God." It is composed of elements that express divine excellence and transcendence. This theophoric name, like many Hebrew names, affirms the nature and greatness of God in the personal identity of the one who bears it.
H3406Q.emploi: In the Bible, at least eleven different men bear the name Jerémoth (or Jérimoth). They appear in various contexts: among the leaders of ancient Benjaminite houses (1 Chronicles 7:8, 7:11, 8:27), among the temple musicians organized in shifts by King David (1 Chronicles 25:22), among royal military officers (1 Chronicles 27:19), and among the descendants of David (2 Chronicles 11:18). The Jerémoth specifically mentioned in Ezra 10:27 is a man from the time of the return from exile who, according to the separation decree issued by Ezra the scribe, had to send away his foreign wife. This same passage also mentions another Jerémoth, son of Zattu, which shows that several men bore the same name and lived at the same time.

sens: Piece of fabric that forms the covering or wall of a tent or building
Decorative element woven, adorned with patterns or colors
Veil that covers and protects something
Covering or envelope in a figurative sense
H3407.detail:
1. The tapis is the main piece of fabric that makes up the structure of a tent or tabernacle. In the descriptions of the Tabernacle, God commands Moses to make ten curtains of fine twisted linen, dyed blue, purple, and scarlet, assembled together to form the walls of the holy dwelling (Exodus 26:1, 26:6). These pieces are joined by gold clasps to form a continuous and solid covering.

2. The tapis can be a finely crafted decorative work. In the Tabernacle, cherubim are artistically depicted on it (Exodus 26:1), showing that it is not just a simple cloth, but a creation woven with care and beauty, reflecting the glory of God.

3. The tapis serves to cover and veil what it envelops, just as God wraps Himself in light like a cloak and stretches out the heavens like a pavilion (Psalms 104:2). This figurative image shows the tapis as protection and majestic adornment.

4. In a figurative sense, the tapis represents an invisible covering or envelope. Jeremiah speaks of the tent that collapses and its tapes that tear (Jeremiah 4:20), an image of destruction and disaster, where even the protective shelter disappears.
H3407.origine: The Hebrew word יְרִיעָה (yeriâh) comes from the verbal root that evokes the idea of suspending or stretching a cloth. It primarily designates a piece of movable and extensible fabric, intended to be stretched and assembled. The plural of the word appears consistently in chapters 26 and 36 of Exodus, showing that the Tabernacle was composed of several curtains sewn together. This word does not have a direct unique equivalent in English: it is rendered sometimes as "tapestry" (when referring to the pieces of the Tabernacle), sometimes as "pavilion" or "tent" (when it designates the entire structure).
H3407.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the Bible, mainly in the chapters dedicated to the construction of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26 and 36), where it designates the pieces of fabric that form the walls of the holy dwelling. Ten tapestries are intended for the walls, others for the doors. It is also encountered in poetic and prophetic contexts: Psalm 104 uses it figuratively for the covering of the heavens ("pavilion"), and the prophets Jeremiah and Habakkuk use it to evoke the destruction of tents and the end of protection (Jeremiah 4:20, 10:20; Habakkuk 3:7). The context determines whether the word designates a concrete material reality or a poetic image.
H3407.portee: For the Christian reader, the tapestry of the Tabernacle reminds us that God does not disdain material details: He commands tapestries woven with artistry and holy colors (blue, purple, scarlet) to honor His dwelling. These tapestries isolate and protect the holy space from the profane world. In a spiritual sense, the image of the heavens as a pavilion stretched by God (Psalms 104:2) invites contemplation of the majesty and vastness of divine creation, visible both as a protective covering and as a demonstration of God's infinite power.

sens: woman of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
wife or concubine of Caleb
H3408.detail: Jerioth is a woman mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:18. She is the wife or concubine of Caleb, son of Hezron, who belonged to the lineage of Judah. The text cites her among the mothers of Caleb's children, alongside Azubah, his wife.
H3408.origine: The name Jerioth literally means "curtains" or "hangings" in Hebrew, derived from the root that designates veils or suspended fabrics. This name may evoke a quality of beauty or ornament, as was often the case for female names of the time. Jerioth lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel.
H3408.emploi: Jerioth appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:18, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. She is mentioned as one of the women of Caleb, son of Hezron. The text lists the sons she bore to Caleb: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. Her appearance in this genealogical context shows that she played an important role in Caleb's family history, even though no other details about her life are provided by Scripture.

sens: The part of the leg between the hip and the knee
The side of a person or an object
The region of the loins, seat of procreative strength
The place where one carried a sword or a weapon
The base or foot of a structure
H3409.detail:
1. The thigh is the fleshy part of the leg, between the hip and the knee. It is the strongest part of the human body. When Abraham asks his servant to put his hand "under his thigh" (Genesis 24:2), it is a gesture of solemn commitment: placing the hand under someone's thigh meant to take an oath, invoking the life and descendants that this part of the body represents.
2. The word also refers to the side, the flank of a person or an object — what is next to it. Thus, the families of Kohath camped "on the southern side of the tabernacle" (Numbers 3:29), and the bronze altar was placed "beside" the new altar (2 Kings 16:14).
3. The loins or kidneys (the region of the thighs) symbolize vital strength and procreative power. This is why descendants are said to be "issued" from the loins of their ancestor: "The people who came with Jacob to Egypt, who were his descendants" (Genesis 46:26).
4. The sword or spear was carried suspended at the thigh. When the text mentions a weapon "at the side" or at the thigh, it recalls the warrior's armament.
5. For an object like the lampstand, the "foot" or base is called thigh — it is the lower support that bears the entire structure (Numbers 8:4).
H3409.origine: The Hebrew word יָרֵךְ (yarekh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of what is "soft" or "flexible." In ancient Semitic culture, the thigh represented the seat of strength, virility, and descent — a notion closely related to life itself. This is why making someone swear by touching under the thigh was an act of deep solemnity. The word then extends to the meaning of "side" (flank of a person or building) and "base" (the lower support).
H3409.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in Genesis and Exodus. Its primary meaning is anatomical: the thigh of the human body. But it also carries significant ritual and symbolic importance. The gesture of placing the hand under a person's thigh to take an oath appears in the accounts of Abraham (Genesis 24:2, 24:9) and continues when Jacob charges Joseph with the same promise (Genesis 47:29). The word extends to the meaning of "side" in descriptions of the tabernacle and its objects (Numbers 3:29, Numbers 8:4, 2 Kings 16:14), and it also designates the weapon carried at the flank (Judges 3:16, Judges 3:21). The usages in the laws of jealousy (Numbers 5:21-27) associate the thigh (the loins) with procreative power, which explains why divine judgment acts there in cases of infidelity.
H3409.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that in the Bible, solemn commitment to God and to others was sealed by gestures laden with meaning. The oath under the thigh showed that the word engaged the entire vital power of the one swearing. This invites reflection on the gravity of the oath and the promise: when one commits before God, it is not an empty formula; it affects our entire life. The word also reminds us that our strength and our descendants come from God alone.

sens: Part of the human body from the hip to the knee
In a statue or representation, the corresponding region
H3410.detail:
1. The thigh is the part of the body between the hip and the knee — the upper part of the leg, fleshy and strong. It is the word used in Daniel 2:32 to describe one of the regions of the body of the colossal statue that King Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream: "its belly and its thighs were of bronze."

2. By extension, the word designates any analogous part in a representation or image of the human body, whether it be a statue, a vision, or a figure.
H3410.origine: This Aramaic word (יַרְכָא, yarka) is an Aramaic form of the corresponding Hebrew word יַרְכָה (yarkah, thigh), which belongs to the same Semitic root. The word evokes the fleshy and visible part of the human body, distinct from the rest of the leg. In Hebrew, the same word appears in various contexts describing the human or animal body.
H3410.emploi: The word appears only once in the Aramaic Bible, in Daniel 2:32, where it is used to describe the statue made of four metals that Nebuchadnezzar saw. In this context, the thigh (of bronze) represents a part of the composite body that symbolizes a succession of kingdoms. It is a simple and concrete anatomical term, without particular nuance.
H3410.portee: This mention of the thighs in Nebuchadnezzar's vision is part of one of the greatest prophecies of the Old Testament concerning the future of earthly empires. It reminds us that the entire human body, in all its parts, was known and visible to God in the detail of this prophetic revelation.

sens: The side, edge, or limit of a place
The far, remote, or deep part of a space
The end of something, its terminal point
The distant region, at the ends of the known world
H3411.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the side or edge of a surface or object: for example, the "western side" of the tabernacle (Exodus 36:27), where the boards of the sanctuary's back were placed. It conveys the idea of a part that extends to the sides.
2. It also refers to depth, the most remote part of a place — the "bottom" that sinks or recedes: the tabernacle thus had its "bottom on the western side," its back and hidden part.
3. From there comes the meaning of extremity in the absolute sense: the farthest place, the point where something stops. Jeremiah speaks of "mighty kings" who "arise from the extremities of the earth" (Jeremiah 50:41) — the borders of the inhabited world.
4. The word can also designate a limit or boundary, as in Zechariah where "the border of Sidon" marks the edge of the territory of Zebulun (Genesis 49:13).
H3411.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of what extends, projects, or stands at a distance. Its etymological link suggests a notion of spreading out or retreating to the sides. In Aramaic, the related word (יַרְכָא) takes on the meaning of "thigh" or "leg," revealing a similar image: the part that moves away or projects from the central body.
H3411.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the Bible, mostly to describe the dimensions of the tabernacle and the temple, or to locate geographical places. In architectural descriptions (Exodus 26 and 36), it designates the "bottom" or the "sides" of sacred structures, particularly on the western side. In geography, it applies to distant regions: the "extremities of Lebanon" (Isaiah 37:24) and the "extremities of the earth" (Jeremiah 50:41, Ezekiel 38:6) represent far-off lands, the borders of the known world. In Psalms 48:3 and 128:3, the word takes on a more tranquil nuance, simply marking a location or territorial limit.
H3411.portee: This word reminds us that God controls all things, from the center to the periphery, from the visible to the distant. When we speak of the "extremities of the earth," we measure the vastness of creation and the scope of divine governance over worlds unknown to us. For the believer, this affirms that no place escapes God, even the most remote corners of the earth.

sens: Canaanite city located in the Lowlands of Judah
Royal city with its own king at the time of the conquest
Fortified place between Hebron and Lachish
H3412G.detail: 1. Jarmuth is a Canaanite city located in the fertile low hills of southern Judah, between Hebron and Lachish (Joshua 15:35). Its name means "heights" in Hebrew, reflecting its geographical position. 2. At the time of Israel's invasion under Joshua, Jarmuth was a royal city governed by its own king. This king allied with four other Canaanite rulers against Israel: the king of Jerusalem, Hebron, Lachish, and Eglon (Joshua 10:3, 10:5). 3. After the defeat of these five kings by Joshua, their bodies were found in a cave and executed (Joshua 10:23). The city is then listed among the cities destroyed during the conquest (Joshua 12:11).
H3412G.origine: The Hebrew name יַרְמוּת (yarmuth) comes from the root רוּם (rum), meaning "to be exalted, high." The name literally means "heights" or "elevated places," likely reflecting the topography of the region. After the conquest, the city retained its importance: it was assigned to Judah and still appears during the time of the temple's reconstruction (Nehemiah 11:29).
H3412G.emploi: Jarmuth appears six times in the Old Testament, primarily in the account of the conquest of the land (the book of Joshua). It is first mentioned as one of the five royal cities that united against Israel during Joshua's advance (Joshua 10:3-5), then as one of the cities whose king was defeated and executed (Joshua 10:23). It is listed among the 31 kings defeated during the conquest (Joshua 12:11). Finally, it appears in the enumeration of cities assigned to Judah and mentioned during the post-exilic reconstruction (Joshua 15:35; Nehemiah 11:29).

sens: Levitical city in the territory of Issachar
H3412H.detail: Jarmuth is a city that was given to the Levites of the Gersonite family. It was located in the territory of Issachar, one of the northern tribes of Israel. Joshua 21:29 mentions it among the cities assigned to the Levitical priests for them to dwell in with their families.
H3412H.origine: The name Jarmuth literally means "heights" in Hebrew. This name likely describes the geographical situation of the city, perched on the heights of the Galilee plateau. Like many ancient place names, it reflects a notable feature of the terrain.
H3412H.emploi: Jarmuth appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 21:29, during the allocation of Levitical cities. It is one of the forty-eight cities given to the Levites scattered throughout the various tribal territories. This system ensured that the priests and worship servants had homes and pastures throughout the promised land.

sens: man from the Exile and Return period
H3413.detail: Jeremiah is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Jewish people returned from exile in Babylon. He is one of the descendants of Hashum who had married foreign women and who, at Ezra's command, had to repudiate these women to comply with the law (Ezra 10:33).
H3413.origine: The Hebrew name יְרֵמַי (Yeremay) literally means "my exaltations" or "my elevations," formed from a root evoking exaltation, greatness, or elevation. It is a theophoric name, meaning a name containing a divine reference, common in Israel.
H3413.emploi: Jeremiah appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:33. He is listed among the men who agreed to separate from their foreign wives during the religious reform led by Ezra after the return from exile in Babylon. His name is grouped with other descendants of Hashum who were in the same situation.

sens: man from Libnah, father of Hamutal
Hamutal was the wife of King Josiah and the mother of kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah
H3414G.detail: 1. Jeremiah is a man from Libnah who lived during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. He is known in the Bible as the father of Hamutal, a woman from the royal house of Judah (2 Kings 23:31). 2. Hamutal, his daughter, married King Josiah and gave birth to at least two kings of Judah: Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. This is why Jeremiah appears in the royal genealogies at the accession of his grandsons to the throne (2 Kings 24:18 and Jeremiah 52:1).
H3414G.origine: The name Jeremiah means "the one whom Jehovah has appointed" or "whom Jehovah has named." In Hebrew, the name combines the idea of God establishing or ordaining something. This name was borne by several men in the Old Testament, the most well-known being the great prophet Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, but this specifically refers to the man from Libnah, father of Hamutal.
H3414G.emploi: Jeremiah appears only three times in the provided biblical texts (2 Kings 23:31, 2 Kings 24:18, and Jeremiah 52:1), and always in the same context: he is presented as the father of Hamutal. His role in the biblical narrative is genealogical: he marks the royal lineage through his daughter who bore kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. He lived in Libnah, a city in the Levant, probably during the reign of King Josiah (late 7th century B.C.).

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh during the time of the divided monarchy
Renowned family leader and valiant warrior
H3414H.detail:
1. Jeremiah is a man belonging to the tribe of Manasseh, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. The text tells us little about him: we know of only one event concerning him, reported in the first book of Chronicles.

2. Jeremiah was a family leader among the Manassites, recognized as a valiant and renowned man. This is why the genealogies of his tribe mention him alongside other family leaders: he represented one of the great families of Manasseh and enjoyed a reputation as a courageous and influential man.
H3414H.origine: The name Jeremiah means "the one whom the Lord has appointed" or "whom the Lord has named." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the action of raising, constituting, or designating someone for a role. This name also gave its name to a well-known man with a significant prophetic mission in the Bible, indicating that the name expressed an idea of destiny and divine calling.
H3414H.emploi: Jeremiah appears only once in Scripture: in 1 Chronicles 5:24. He is listed in the genealogical record of the descendants of Manasseh, in Transjordan (east of the Jordan). He is presented alongside other valiant and renowned men, leaders of their respective paternal houses. His sole mention shows that he was a respected figure in his region and tribe, but no particular act is recorded about him. Unlike other biblical characters bearing the same name, this one is known only by his place in the genealogy of Israel.

sens: Warrior of David who joined him at Ziklag
H3414I.detail: 1. This is a man who was among the military companions of King David. According to the text of 1 Chronicles 12:4, Jeremiah is listed among the valiant warriors who rallied to David at Ziklag, the reinforcement the king received before ascending to the throne of Israel.
H3414I.origine: The name Jeremiah (Hebrew יִרְמְיָ֫הוּ, yirmeyahu) means "the one whom Jehovah has raised" or "whom Jehovah has appointed"; it comes from the root that evokes the action of lifting, elevating. It is a name bearing a promise: the one who bears it is placed by God himself in a prominent position. Although the name is most commonly associated with the great prophet Jeremiah, several men bore it in the history of Israel.
H3414I.emploi: The Jeremiah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 12:4 is one of the warriors who supported David during his flight and rise to royalty. He appears only in this verse, listed among the valiant who aligned themselves under David's authority. The context indicates a man of war, part of an elite military recognized for its valor.

sens: Warrior of David, from the tribe of Gad
H3414J.detail: 1. Jeremiah is a man from the tribe of Gad who rallied to David at Ziklag, while David was fleeing from King Saul. He is mentioned in the list of valiant warriors who joined David: "Mischmanna, the fourth; Jeremiah, the fifth" (1 Chronicles 12:10). He is a faithful soldier among the king's champions.
H3414J.origine: The name literally means "whom Jehovah has appointed" or "whom Jehovah has named." It is a theophoric name—a name constructed with the divine name—very common in Israel to express that God has placed this child in a particular role. The name is borne by several men in the Bible, the most famous being the great prophet Jeremiah, son of the priest Hilkiah.
H3414J.emploi: Jeremiah is a warrior from Gad mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 12:10. He is among the valiant men of war who attached themselves to David at Ziklag when he was pursued by Saul. He is simply one of the many devoted soldiers who supported David in his exile and contributed to the formation of his victorious army.

sens: Man from the time of the Divided Monarchy, mentioned only once in Chronicles
H3414K.detail: 1. Jeremiah is a warrior of David, mentioned in the list of men who joined him at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:13). He is presented as the tenth in a enumeration of valiant warriors. This character appears only in this verse and remains less known compared to other figures of David, but he is among those who supported the king in his battles.
H3414K.origine: The name "Jeremiah" means "the one whom the Lord has appointed" or "whom the Lord has named," formed from the root רוּם (to raise, to establish) and the divine יָה (Yah). This name carries the idea of a destiny set by God. Several men bear this name in Scripture, but this Jeremiah is a simple Davidic warrior, very different from the great prophet Jeremiah son of Hilkiah.
H3414K.emploi: This Jeremiah appears only once in 1 Chronicles 12:13, in the list of warriors who joined David at Ziklag after he fled from Saul. His name is listed tenth among these valiant men. Unlike the prophet Jeremiah who marked the history of Israel with his words and sufferings, this man remains a secondary figure, simply identified by his role as a faithful warrior to King David.

sens: The great prophet of Israel who preached during the end of the Kingdom of Judah
Son of the priest Hilkiah, from Anathoth
Author of the prophetic book that bears his name
Man persecuted for announcing God's judgment on Jerusalem
H3414L.detail:
1. Jeremiah is the major prophet of the Old Testament, contemporary with the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. He spoke the words of God for over forty years, calling the people to repentance. The book of Jeremiah, one of the longest in the Bible, records his oracles and his troubled life (Jeremiah 1:1, 25:2).
2. Jeremiah was the son of the priest Hilkiah, and he belonged to the priestly family of Anathoth, a town near Jerusalem. This priestly background marked him and prepared him for his prophetic ministry.
3. God called him to preach an unpopular message: the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians and the exile of the people. Unlike the false prophets who promised peace, Jeremiah announced disaster and invasion (Jeremiah 28 shows his conflict with the prophet Hananiah).
4. Because of this message, Jeremiah suffered horrible persecutions: imprisoned, thrown into a cistern, beaten, mocked. His enemies sought to kill him, but God protected him (Jeremiah 36:26, 37:15, 38:6-11). His faithfulness in suffering makes him a model of prophetic courage.
H3414L.origine: The name Jeremiah means "whom the Lord has appointed" or "exalted of the Lord" (from Yahu, the divine name, and from the root "to raise, to name"). This name reflects the divine calling on his life. Other characters bear this name in the Old Testament, but none have had the significance of Jeremiah the great prophet. In Greek (the language of the New Testament), his name is written Hieremias.
H3414L.emploi: Jeremiah appears 121 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the book that bears his name (62 chapters). He is first mentioned in 2 Chronicles 35:25, where the text notes that he composed a lament for the death of King Josiah. He also appears in 2 Chronicles at the time of the fall of Jerusalem, and in Ezra at the return from exile. The heart of his story is found in the book of Jeremiah: his calls to repentance, his conflicts with false prophets, his sufferings in prison, and the oracles of hope he proclaimed even during the siege of the city. His disciples, including the scribe Baruch, helped him preserve his words.
H3414L.portee: Jeremiah teaches believers faithfulness to God even when it is unpopular and costly. His life shows that the prophet must never soften God's message to please human ears, but announce the truth with courage. Through his laments and letters of exile, Jeremiah also reveals a God who never delivers His people to eternal destruction: even judgment is a step toward forgiveness and restoration. For the Christian, Jeremiah is an example of perseverance in God's calling in the face of obstacles.

sens: Priest of Judah who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H3414M.detail: 1. Jeremiah is a name borne by several characters in the Old Testament, but here it refers to a priest who returned from Babylon when the Jews were freed after the exile. He is mentioned alongside Zerubbabel and Joshua (Nehemiah 12:1). He represents a figure of restoration: the people of God return to their land and their religious structures are reestablished. This Jeremiah is among the heads of priestly families at the time of Governor Nehemiah, notably at the time of the renewal of the covenant (Nehemiah 10:2), and is identified as one of the leaders under the high priest Jehoiakim (Nehemiah 12:12).
H3414M.origine: The name Jeremiah means "whom the Lord has appointed" or "whom the Lord has named." It comes from the Hebrew verb "rûm" which evokes elevation, establishment. The name expresses the idea that a person receives their charge and authority from God. Several biblical characters bear this name, all linked to important moments in Israel's history.
H3414M.emploi: This Jeremiah (distinct from the great prophet) appears four times in the book of Nehemiah, between 445 and 420 B.C. He is a priest and is among those who sign the covenant of religious reform in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 10:2). He is part of the priests who returned from exile with Zerubbabel one or two generations earlier (Nehemiah 12:1), and is counted among the heads of priestly houses at the time of the high priest Jehoiakim. His name also appears in a list of those surrounding Nehemiah during the dedication of the walls.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah mentioned during the time of the kings of Israel and Judah
H3414N.detail: 1. This Jeremiah is the father of Jaazaniah and the son of Habaziniah. He is cited only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 35:3, where the prophet Jeremiah mentions him while presenting Jaazaniah and his family, who belong to the house of the Rechabites—a community known for its austere lifestyle and obedience to God.
H3414N.origine: The name Jeremiah comes from the Hebrew yir-me-yah, composed of two elements: yir ("to name," "to call") and Yah (the abbreviated divine name). Its literal meaning is "the one whom Yahweh has named" or "whom Jehovah has appointed." This name evokes the idea of a person designated or chosen by God for a particular function or responsibility.
H3414N.emploi: This Jeremiah appears only once in Scripture: in Jeremiah 35:3. He is presented as the father of Jaazaniah, a man from the house of the Rechabites. Although the text does not describe him directly, his belonging to a family known for its adherence to divine laws and moral integrity suggests that he was a man of principle. He should not be confused with the great prophet Jeremiah, author of the book that bears the same name.

sens: To have a troubled heart, to be pained, immersed in sadness
To be seized with fear, dread, or distress
To bear an emotional burden that affects well-being
H3415.detail:
1. To have a troubled heart, to be pained, immersed in sadness: the word denotes an inner state of deep sorrow. Hannah, the mother of Samuel, is a perfect example — her husband notices that she is not eating and asks why her heart is "saddened" (1 Samuel 1:8). It is the sadness that weighs on someone to the point of affecting their body and behavior.

2. To be seized with fear, dread, or distress: the word can also evoke an inner fright, an emotional disturbance caused by fear. In Isaiah 15:4, the warriors of Moab have "fear in their soul" — an anxiety in the face of imminent danger that paralyzes them morally.

3. To bear an emotional burden that affects well-being: in all cases, the word paints a deep disturbance of the soul, which is not just a fleeting feeling but marks the person from within.
H3415.origine: The Hebrew verb יָרַע comes from a root expressing the idea of trembling or vibrating internally. The starting image is that of agitation, a physical or emotional disturbance — like a tremor that shakes the body. This same root appears in other contexts where it describes a violent emotion or a bodily reaction to distress.
H3415.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament (including these two usages provided). In 1 Samuel 1:8, it characterizes Hannah's emotional state, barren and suffering, whose heart has become "saddened." In Isaiah 15:4, it describes the moral distress of the warriors of Moab in the face of military threat. In both contexts, the word paints an intense emotion that overwhelms the person — not mere melancholy, but a deep and manifest disturbance.
H3415.portee: This word teaches us that sadness and fear are human realities that the Bible does not hide. Hannah, beloved of her husband, remains saddened by her desire for a child — and God sees this pain, listens to her, and gives her Samuel. The Bible validates our sorrows while reminding us that God is present in distress. This encourages the believer not to hide their true emotions but to bring them before God in prayer.

sens: City of the tribe of Benjamin, in the Promised Land
H3416.detail: Jirpeel is a small city assigned to the tribe of Benjamin during the division of the Promised Land. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities of Benjamin (Joshua 18:27), where it appears between Rekem and Thareala.
H3416.origine: The Hebrew name יִרְפְּאֵל (yir-pe-él) literally means "God will heal" or "God will cure." It is composed of the root רְפָא (rephá), which means "to heal," and the divine name אֵל (El), "God." This name expresses a trust in divine healing, characteristic of place names in ancient Israel.
H3416.emploi: Jirpeel is a minor city of Benjamin, mentioned only once in Joshua 18:27, at the time when Joshua is distributing territories to the twelve tribes after the conquest of Canaan. It is part of the list of cities assigned to Benjamin, alongside other less significant localities of the tribal territory. Its exact location is not precisely identified by archaeologists.

sens: To expel saliva from the mouth as a sign of contempt or dishonor
To publicly mark someone with infamy or humiliation
H3417.detail: 1. Spitting in someone's face is to reject their saliva upon them, a violent and humiliating gesture that expresses absolute contempt. In Numbers 12:14, the Lord says that if Miriam's own father had spit in her face, she would be dishonored for seven days: the spit is the image of shame and public repulsion. 2. This gesture becomes a legal and public act of repudiation in the context of the levirate law (Deuteronomy 25:9): the sister-in-law spits in the face of the brother who refuses to perpetuate the name of his deceased brother. It is a visible verdict of infamy pronounced before witnesses, which freezes in memory the dishonor of the one refusing.
H3417.origine: The Hebrew verb yaraq denotes the physical action of spitting. It belongs to a small family of concrete words related to the mouth and projections (like yarok, the green, which evokes the bursting forth). Spitting is a primitive, universal gesture of repulsion and rejection: in a biblical context, it carries a legal and covenantal dimension, as dishonor touches on the continuity of lineage and fidelity to the dead.
H3417.emploi: The verb to spit appears only twice in the Old Testament, always in a context of law and shame. In Numbers 12:14, it illustrates the sanction that Miriam would have deserved for her rebellion against Moses: the spit symbolizes judgment and temporary exclusion from the people. In Deuteronomy 25:9, it is codified as part of the ritual of denouncing a refusal of levirate duty: the woman spits to publicly testify to the infamy of the man and his rejection of familial obligation. In both cases, spitting is an official, solemn act pronounced before witnesses.
H3417.portee: This word reminds the reader that dishonor and shame are serious realities in God's covenant with Israel. Spitting, a physical gesture of aversion, reveals how the sins of pride (Miriam) or malice towards the dead and lineage (the refusing brother) harm the holy people. It is a call to faithfulness to the order that God has established and to the memory of the dead.

sens: That which is green in color, the hue of nature that grows
Greenness, grass and green plants
Grass or foliage as food for animals
That which is young, vigorous, fresh
By extension, that which is fragile and ephemeral
H3418.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the color green itself, that which is seen in living nature. In Genesis 1:30, God gives all the animals "every green herb for food": it is the characteristic hue of plant life at the time of its growth.
2. It then applies to greenness as a whole: the grass of the fields, the plants, the vegetation that covers the ground. In Exodus 10:15, after the plague of locusts, "there remained no greenness on the trees nor in the grass of the fields" in Egypt.
3. The greenness also served as pasture for the beasts. In Numbers 22:4, Balak fears that Israel will consume "the greenness of the fields" as "the ox grazes."
4. The adjective also evokes that which is young and vigorous: in Psalms 37:2, the wicked are "cut down as quickly as the green grass," a symbol of fragility and brevity.
5. The greenness disappears and withers: in Isaiah 15:6, "the grass is withered, the greenness has disappeared," an image of death and divine judgment.
H3418.origine: The Hebrew word יֶרֶק (yerek) comes from a root that means properly "to be green." It belongs to the same family as other words describing growth and youth. In Hebrew, the color green is that of life sprouting, of spring and fertility. This word reflects the biblical vision of the created world, where greenness is a sign of divine order and God's blessing on His creation.
H3418.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of natural life or sustenance. At the beginning of Genesis, it describes the food that God designates for all living beings (Genesis 1:30 and 9:3), marking divine abundance and provision. In the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 10:15), the locusts destroy all greenness, showing God's power over nature and punishment. In Numbers 22:4, Balak worries that the people of Israel will exhaust the verdant resources. Finally, biblical poetry uses greenness and green grass to express transience: in Psalms 37:2, the wicked wither like green grass, and in Isaiah 15:6, its disappearance symbolizes ruin and divine judgment. The word thus circulates between the real image of plant life and a metaphorical significance of fragility.
H3418.portee: The term reminds us of God's creation and His generosity: every green plant testifies that God provides for all the needs of His creatures. It also invites us to meditate on the ephemeral: the greenness that seems robust wilts in an instant, just like the existence of those who turn away from God. This contrast calls the believer to place their hope not in what passes away, but in the One who remains.

sens: Herbaceous plant that grows spontaneously or is cultivated for food
Tender and fresh greenery of a plant at the beginning of its growth
Garden or land arranged to grow vegetables and herbs
Everything that is fragile, ephemeral, and without strength
H3419.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to edible herbs and vegetables, the plants that are cultivated for nourishment — it is the grass that is sown and watered. In Deuteronomy 11:10, it refers to the Egyptian garden that the Israelites watered with their hands, or the small garden that King Ahab covets next to his house (1 Kings 21:2).
2. The word depicts the tender greenery that grows in spring, the young foliage full of life — this tender grass described in Isaiah 37:27, before it dries up and withers away.
3. The word can also refer to a vegetable garden or cultivated land itself, a garden where these plants grow — like the one Ahab wants to make where Naboth's vineyard was.
4. In a striking image, the Bible uses this word to describe what is fragile and without strength: the powerless inhabitants of Jerusalem are compared to tender grass that withers, weak and ephemeral in the face of God's power (2 Kings 19:26 and Isaiah 37:27).
H3419.origine: The Hebrew word yarak comes from a root that evokes greenness and moisture. It paints the image of what is alive and green — the plant that needs water and grows. The family of the word includes herbs that express tenderness, freshness, and growth. This simple and concrete word shows how Hebrew directly names what man cultivates to live.
H3419.emploi: This word appears five times in the provided biblical text: twice referring to gardens (Deuteronomy and 1 Kings), where it designates the garden specifically arranged to feed the household; twice referring to tender greenery (2 Kings and Isaiah), in a poetic comparison that emphasizes the fragility of enemies before God; once in a proverb (Proverbs 15:17), where the simple grass of the poor contrasts with the fattened ox of the rich — not to despise wealth, but to say that love is better than abundance. The word thus oscillates between the concrete (the cultivated garden) and the figurative (the grass that is allowed to die to signify human fragility).
H3419.portee: This word invites the believer to see in the fragility of grass a lesson in humility: man, despite his apparent strength, is as ephemeral as the green grass that dries up. But it also says that simple life — of bread and grass with love — is richer than a luxurious life without love. It is a quiet wisdom that measures true riches.

sens: disease that attacks grains and destroys the harvest
rust or rot that spoils plants
paleness or yellowish tint of the face
absence of color and life
H3420.detail:
1. Blight is an agricultural scourge that strikes the harvests: a disease of grains and herbs that causes them to wither and disappear. It appears in the lists of punishments that God sends to His unfaithful people, alongside famine, rust, and locusts (Amos 4:9, Haggai 2:17).
2. In a close sense, it also refers to rust or rot that corrodes plants — fruits, vines, fig trees, olive trees — and devours them (1 Kings 8:37, 2 Chronicles 6:28).
3. By extension, the word describes the paleness or discoloration of the human face, this lack of brightness and color that betrays fear, suffering, or illness. Jeremiah asks: "Why have all faces turned pale?" (Jeremiah 30:6).
4. This pale or yellowish tint symbolizes collapse and death: the face emptied of its life, struck by anguish or evil (Deuteronomy 28:22).
H3420.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes paleness, sickly greenness, and withering. The basic image is that of color fading or turning yellow-greenish: first on plants affected by a disease, then on the human face emptied of its strength. The word translates everything that is pale, wilted, or eaten away by illness.
H3420.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of plagues and punishments. In the Law (Deuteronomy), it is among the plagues that God sends to the people who forsake Him. In the times of the kings, the prayer accounts (1 Kings 8, 2 Chronicles 6) mention it as a danger to which the harvests are exposed. The prophets (Jeremiah, Amos, Haggai) use it to describe both the destruction of crops and the ravaged, pale appearance of men struck by misfortune. It is a word of lament and alarm.
H3420.portee: This word reminds us that disease, plague, and physical destruction are both a reality of the created world and a language by which God speaks to His people. The blight that ravages the harvests or pales the face manifests the absence of divine blessing — it calls for repentance and a return to God.

sens: Character from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H3421.detail: Jorkeam is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in the genealogy of the Calebites (descendants of Caleb), an important lineage of Judah. His father is Raham, and he is cited in the series of descendants of Shebal (1 Chronicles 2:44).
H3421.origine: His name literally means "the empty people." It is a typical Hebrew compound name, formed from words that evoke absence or emptiness, although its deep meaning and historical context elude us.
H3421.emploi: Jorkeam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:44. He is listed in a long genealogy of the descendants of Caleb after the conquest of Canaan. These genealogical lists served to establish land rights and inheritance of the tribes and families in Israel. The fact that he is explicitly named, even once, shows that he retained some importance in the genealogical memory of his family.

sens: Having a pale or whitish green tint
Tending towards yellow-green
Reminiscent of the color of certain diseases or skin conditions
H3422.detail:
1. This word describes a pale and indefinite color, leaning towards green without having its intensity. In the law concerning leprosy, the priest examines the sores on clothing or skin: if they are "greenish" or reddish, it is a sign of leprous contamination (Leviticus 13:49). The same suspicious tint can appear on the walls of a house, indicating mold or infection (Leviticus 14:37).
2. The tint can also lean towards yellow-green, like a faded or wilted color. The psalmist speaks of the dove's wings covered with silver, whose plumage shines with a "yellow" of gold (Psalms 68:14) — here the word denotes a golden shine mixed with green, characteristic of iridescent plumage.
3. This color often evokes disease, alteration, degeneration: it is the hue of what rots, alters, or disintegrates, hence its frequent use to diagnose leprosy and impurity.
H3422.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes paleness and green. It is formed by reduplication (yéraqraq), a common process in Hebrew to intensify a quality or nuance it. The simple root designates green and strangulation (hence the paleness of the sick). This formation emphasizes the indefinite, pale, or changing aspect of the hue.
H3422.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in passages of priestly law concerning purity. Two uses concern the diagnosis of leprosy: it manifests through greenish sores on clothing (Leviticus 13:49) and on the walls of houses (Leviticus 14:37), where it is accompanied by sunken cavities. A poetic use describes the dove whose plumage reflects a gold-green tint (Psalms 68:14). The medical and ritual context dominates: it is a color of alert, impurity, or alteration.
H3422.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not shy away from confronting the reality of disease and evil, including its visible and unpleasant signs. The greenish color signals an impurity that God invites us to examine, recognize, and address — not to ignore or deny. For the Christian, it is an invitation to name and confront sin and its consequences rather than camouflage them.

sens: To take possession of land or property
To inherit something from a parent or previous generation
To occupy a place, to settle there
To become poor, to be dispossessed
To destroy, to bring to nothing
H3423G.detail:
1. To take possession of land or property means to seize it for oneself, to conquer it or to appropriate it: Abraham asks God who will be his heir since he has no child (Genesis 15:3), and the Psalms speak of those who hope in the Lord and will possess the land (Psalms 37:9).

2. To inherit means to receive property, land, or a title from a father or a preceding generation: the daughters of Israel who have an inheritance must keep it within their family by marrying appropriately, so that each one possesses the inheritance of their fathers (Numbers 36:8).

3. To occupy or dwell in a place means to take possession by settling there: the hedgehog and the pelican will possess the desolate land, meaning they will seize it and inhabit it (Isaiah 34:11).

4. To become poor or to be dispossessed means to lose one's possessions or to be reduced to poverty: the word can also mean impoverishment, the opposite of possession.

5. To destroy or to bring to nothing means to completely devastate: Ezekiel speaks of those who claim to possess the land while committing abominations that defile it (Ezekiel 33:25-26).
H3423G.origine: The Hebrew verb yasha' (יָרַשׁ) fundamentally expresses the action of seizing, taking, and keeping for oneself. Its root evokes the occupation of a space, both physical and legal. The word belongs to the semantic family of inheritance and succession: it describes the transfer of property from one generation to another, or the conquest of new land. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it often translates the Greek verb κληρονομέω (kléronoméô), which also carries the meaning of inheriting.
H3423G.emploi: This verb appears 34 times in the Old Testament. It is particularly frequent in the Psalms (where those who hope in the Lord will possess the land) and in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Amos), where the promise of possession of the land is linked to faithfulness to God and eternal inheritance. The context varies: legal and familial possession (Numbers 36:8), divine promise of land (1 Chronicles 28:8), destruction of enemy peoples (Isaiah 34:11), or eschatological promise to the faithful (Psalms 37:9-29). The meaning can also shift towards impoverishment or dispossession depending on the verb forms used.
H3423G.portee: For the biblical reader, this word carries the central promise that God gives to His people: not only a physical land but an eternal possession linked to the inheritance of faith. To possess is never an isolated act: it is to receive from God and then to pass on to future generations. This invites the believer to see their life and possessions as a deposit received, for which they will give an account and which they will pass on, not by their own right but by divine grace.

sens: To seize something, to take ownership
To drive out the inhabitants of a place to become its master
To inherit something after someone
To become poor, to be dispossessed of one's goods
H3423H.detail:
1. To seize something, to take ownership: the word designates the action of taking possession of a property, conquering it, or occupying it. Genesis 15:7 gives the clearest image: God promises Abram to give him the land in "possession," meaning as property that will be his.
2. To drive out the inhabitants of a place to become its master: this is the most frequent usage in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the account of the conquest. Deuteronomy 11:23 shows this: "the Lord will drive out before you all these nations," and thus Israel will take possession. The word evokes both expulsion and takeover.
3. To inherit something after someone: to possess something as an heir. This is a nuance of the previous meaning, but applied to the transmission between generations or succession within a family.
4. To become poor, to be dispossessed of one's goods: this is a less common but attested meaning; the word can also signify the opposite: to be impoverished, to lose one's wealth and status. This nuance reflects the idea that one who loses their property also loses their dignity and stability.
H3423H.origine: The word comes from an ancient Hebrew root that expresses the idea of seizing, taking with force. The family of the word includes derivatives that speak of inheritance, possession, and poverty—all linked to the idea of control or loss of control over property. The basic image is that of a hand that seizes: one "takes" a land, a property, an inheritance. It is a central verb in the biblical vocabulary of conquest and covenant.
H3423H.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, with about 167 occurrences.
