H3452H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be empty" or "to be desolate." It literally describes a place without inhabitants, a region devoid of what sustains life. The Hebrew term emphasizes emptiness and absence rather than danger or heat.
H3452H.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and the Pentateuch. It first designates specific geographical regions of Moab or Sinai (Numbers). But it gradually takes on a broader and more spiritual meaning: the desert becomes the symbol of a time of trial and doubt, where God tests the faithfulness of His people. The Psalms use it to evoke Israel's murmurs in the desert — a historical event that has become an image of perpetual temptation.
H3452H.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that trials and apparent desolation can be places of encounter with God. The desert is not just an obstacle: it is the place where God keeps His people and shapes them. This invites us to see the trials of life as spaces where God acts, provided we trust Him rather than murmur.

sens: Old man, advanced in age
Person who has accumulated the experience of many years
Figure of wisdom and authority in the community
H3453.detail: 1. An elder is a man who has grown old, marked by age and often by gray hair: Job 15:10 speaks of "gray hair" and "elders" to designate the oldest men. 2. The word also designates one who has lived long and therefore possesses a deep knowledge of things: Job 12:12 asserts that "wisdom is with the aged," suggesting that age naturally brings intelligence and understanding. 3. In the social and religious life of Israel, the elder embodies authority and respect: Job 29:8 shows that young men withdrew and elders stood up to honor the one who spoke, revealing their status as prominent figures to whom honor is given.
H3453.origine: The Hebrew word יָשִׁישׁ comes from a root that expresses the idea of being old, worn by time. The root evokes the accumulation of years and the gradual degeneration that results. It is not a technical term but a simple and direct description of one whose body and experience have been shaped by decades.
H3453.emploi: This word appears four times in the book of Job, always to designate older men. Job contrasts the elders with the young: sometimes to assert that the elders possess wisdom (Job 12:12 and 15:10), sometimes to show the respect given to them (Job 29:8), and sometimes to establish a hierarchy of age and authority (Job 32:6, where Elihu, young, humbles himself before the elders). The word always designates a living man, never an abstraction, and emphasizes both the physical aspect of age and the social and moral dimension that age confers.
H3453.portee: The word elder reminds us that in the Bible, age is not a diminishment or decline to be feared, but a richness. The years bring wisdom and discernment, and society should honor its elders. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to respect the experience of those who have gone before us and to recognize that a long life is a gift from God filled with meaning.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H3454.detail: Jeshishai is a man belonging to the tribe of Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of the Gadites of Gilead. His name appears in a long family lineage, where he is the son of Jachdo and the father of Michael.
H3454.origine: The Hebrew name יְשִׁישַׁי literally means "my old one" or "my elder," formed from the root שׁישׁ which expresses the idea of old age or longevity. This type of name, common in ancient Israel, could be given to express a quality or situation at the time of the child's birth.
H3454.emploi: Jeshishai is cited only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 5:14, where he appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Gad. This unique usage places him in the time of the divided monarchy in Israel, and he is presented as a member of the tribe settled in Gilead, a rich and fertile region east of the Jordan.

sens: Place something somewhere
Deposit an object in a place or a container
Put someone in a situation or a role
H3455.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of the action of placing or positioning an object: one puts something in a specific place. In Genesis 50:26, they put Joseph's body in a coffin — it literally refers to depositing his embalmed body in this funeral container.
2. The verb can also mean to install or entrust something to a place or someone, with the idea that the thing will remain there or fulfill its function.
3. Figuratively, to put can mean to establish someone in a position, role, or situation: to appoint, institute, create a relationship.
H3455.origine: The verb יָשַׂם comes from an ancient Hebrew root expressing the simple and concrete action of "to place" or "to put." This verb is common in the Old Testament to express actions of positioning, whether material or metaphorical. The root evokes the image of a hand placing an object, of a decision that puts something in place.
H3455.emploi: This verb appears only once in the provided usages, in Genesis 50:26, where it describes the practical and concrete action of placing Joseph's embalmed body in a coffin. It is a classic usage of the verb in its literal and direct sense: putting an object (the body) in a container (the coffin) in Egypt, where Joseph spent his life as a slave and minister to Pharaoh.
H3455.portee: This simple verb reminds us how the Bible reports the most human events, even the gravest, with realism and sobriety. The detail that Joseph is "put" in a coffin in Egypt, before his promise of resurrection and return to the promised land, underscores the humility of the body in death — but also the certainty that God fulfills His promises beyond the grave.

sens: To be reduced to a state of ruin and abandonment
To be ugly, emptied of its inhabitants and life
To cause ruin and devastation
To annihilate, completely destroy
H3456.detail:
1. The word denotes the state of a land or city transformed into ruins, abandoned and barren. In Genesis 47:19, the Egyptians fear that their lands will become "desolate," meaning they will cease to be cultivated and productive, left to abandonment.
2. The image evokes a landscape emptied of life: no more inhabitants, no more noise, no more activity. It is the state of a devastated dwelling that is filled only with silence and death.
3. The verb can also express the action of causing this ruin. In Ezekiel 6:6, God announces that the cities will be "devastated," their temples and idols "forsaken and abandoned."
4. When the word is used for a destructive action (Ezekiel 19:7), it means to annihilate: "He destroyed their cities," ravaging everything that was there, like a furious lion ravages a flock.
H3456.origine: The Hebrew root ישׁם evokes the idea of emptiness and absence. It is related to words meaning "to make silent" or "to be silent," reflecting the atmosphere of death and abandonment that characterizes a desolate land. The word belongs to a semantic family of destruction and ruin that permeates the prophets of doom.
H3456.emploi: The verb appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, first in Genesis 47:19, where it describes the fear of an abandoned and barren land during the famine. It then becomes very frequent in the prophecies of Ezekiel, where it expresses God's judgment: destroyed lands (Ezekiel 6:6, 12:19), cities reduced to nothing (Ezekiel 19:7). In these prophetic contexts, the word carries a grave solemnity: it is the punishment that strikes idolatry and injustice.
H3456.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the consequences of sin and abandonment of God. Desolation is never simply a physical catastrophe; it is the silence that follows judgment, the death of a civilization that has turned away. But it also reminds us that God controls history: only His will can destroy or restore. For the Christian, it serves as a warning against idolatry and an invitation to seek life in God alone.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah
Son of Hur
Brother of Jizreel and other children of Hur
H3457.detail: Jishma is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:3. His name means "desolation" in Hebrew. He is presented as one of the sons of Hur, alongside his brothers Jizreel and Jidbasch, and his sister Hatselelponi. This genealogical passage is part of the list of descendants of Judah, tracing back to the time of Egypt and the desert.
H3457.origine: The name Jishma comes from Hebrew and literally means "desolation." It belongs to an important family of Judah, that of Hur, which has marked the history of the people. The genealogical context shows that Jishma is part of a lineage of leaders and important figures from the tribe of Judah.
H3457.emploi: Jishma appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:3, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. He is presented as one of the sons of Hur, brother of Jizreel and Jidbasch. This genealogy places Jishma among the important ancestors of Judah, although his personal life is not reported in the biblical text. His unique appearance shows that despite his family importance, few details are transmitted about him.

sens: Son of Abraham and Hagar, ancestor of the Arab peoples
Son of Nethaniah, murderer of Gedaliah
H3458G.detail:
1. Ishmael is the son that Abraham had with Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian servant. He is the one whom the angel announces to Hagar, telling her that God has heard her distress (Genesis 16:11). He becomes the father of twelve sons and the leader of a great people in the desert, according to the promise made to Abraham: "I will bless him, I will make him fruitful, and he will become a great nation" (Genesis 17:20). Ishmael lived one hundred thirty-seven years and was gathered to his people after his death (Genesis 25:17).
2. Another Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, is mentioned in the later historical books. He plays a much less benevolent role: he murders Gedaliah, the governor whom Nebuchadnezzar had established in Judah after the destruction of the Temple.
H3458G.origine: The name means "God will hear" or "God has heard" in Hebrew: it is composed of "El" (God) and "shama" (to hear). It is a name of promise, given because the Lord answered Hagar's cry of distress in the desert. The name recalls divine intervention and God's compassion towards a rejected woman. Several biblical characters bear this name, but the most famous remains the son of Abraham.
H3458G.emploi: Ishmael, son of Abraham, is mentioned early in Genesis to recount how Abraham, doubting the divine promise, accepted to take Hagar and father a son with her. This child is born when Abraham is eighty-six years old (Genesis 16:16), and Isaac, the child of promise, will not come until thirteen years later. Ishmael is circumcised at the age of thirteen when Abraham is ninety-nine (Genesis 17:25). After Isaac's birth, Hagar and Ishmael are sent away into the desert, but God promises that Ishmael will also become the leader of a great people (Genesis 17:20). The genealogical lists enumerate Ishmael's twelve sons and his descendants (Genesis 25:12-16), who occupy the territories of the Arabian desert. Ishmael participates in Abraham's burial alongside Isaac (Genesis 25:9).
H3458G.portee: The story of Ishmael shows God's mercy towards those who are cast aside or forgotten. Although Ishmael is not the heir of the promise of salvation, God does not abandon him and blesses him. For the Christian reader, this story reveals that God watches over all, even over children born from our doubts or unfaithfulness. It also invites us to recognize that all blessings come from God, but that some promises are particular and exclusive.

sens: son of Nethaniah, military leader who assassinated Gedaliah
H3458H.detail: Ishmael is a military leader who appears after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. He is first presented as one of the captains who remained loyal to the governor Gedaliah established by the Babylonians (2 Kings 25:23). But Ishmael secretly plots against Gedaliah: warned by Johanan that the king of the Ammonites has charged him with killing him, Ishmael organizes a pretense meal, then assassinates Gedaliah, his guard, and the Babylonian soldiers present (Jeremiah 41:1-3). He throws their corpses into an ancient cistern (Jeremiah 41:9). Pursued by Johanan and his troops whom he had captured as hostages, he flees to Transjordan (Jeremiah 41:12-15). His act of treachery and murder hinders the reconstruction of Judah and forces the survivors to seek refuge in Egypt.
H3458H.origine: The name means "God will hear" in Hebrew (from "God" and "to hear"). It is the same name borne by the son of Abraham and Hagar in Genesis, ancestor of the Arab peoples. In our usages, it designates a historical figure from the 6th century B.C., a military leader of post-exilic Judah.
H3458H.emploi: Ishmael appears in the account of the events that followed the destruction of Jerusalem. The passages in Jeremiah 40 and 41 detail how this son of Nethaniah, a warrior leader, deceived Gedaliah with a peace meal, then killed him with his men, threw the corpses into a cistern (Jeremiah 41:9), and took the survivors hostage before fleeing from Johanan's army. He symbolizes the internal conflicts that tore Judah apart at its greatest weakness. His story illustrates how pride and ambition destroy the last efforts of reconstruction.
H3458H.portee: The story of Ishmael reminds us that treachery and violence divide an already broken people. It shows how bitterness and the thirst for power can drive a man to commit the unthinkable, even against those who work for peace. It invites the reader to meditate on the necessity of forgiveness and unity in times of crisis.

sens: Benjamite, son of Azel and grandson of Saul
H3458I.detail: 1. Ishmael is a Benjamite mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is one of the six sons of Azel and therefore a grandson of Saul through the line of Meribbaal (or Mephibosheth). He appears in the two parallel passages in Chronicles that list his family descent.
H3458I.origine: The Hebrew name Ishmael (יִשְׁמָעֵאל) means "God will hear." It is formed from two elements: El (God) and Shama (to hear, to listen). This name expresses confidence that God listens to the calls and prayers of the one who bears it. Although this Benjamite bears the same name as Ishmael, the son of Abraham (the father of the Arab peoples), they are different men living in very distant historical periods.
H3458I.emploi: This Benjamite named Ishmael appears only twice in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44, in two nearly identical genealogical lists enumerating the sons of Azel. These passages are likely variants of the same document or copies of one another, serving to trace the royal lineage of the tribe of Benjamin after the exile. No particular event from his life is reported.

sens: Father of Zebadiah, chief of the house of Judah during the reign of Jehoshaphat
H3458J.detail: Ishmael is a man from the time of the divided monarchy in Judah, known only by the mention of his son Zebadiah in 2 Chronicles 19:11. He is identified as the father of this Zebadiah who held a position of authority in the house of Judah, meaning he oversaw the affairs of the king during the reign of King Jehoshaphat.
H3458J.origine: The name Ishmael means "God will hear" in Hebrew. It comes from the root שׁמע ("to hear") and the name of God אל. This same name has been borne by several characters in biblical history, including the son of Abraham and Hagar, ancestor of the Arab peoples, but also by several other men in the following generations, as here.
H3458J.emploi: Ishmael is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 19:11. On this occasion, he is presented as the father of Zebadiah, who exercised authority in the government of Judah under King Jehoshaphat. This Zebadiah was in charge of the king's affairs, working alongside the high priest Amaria who handled religious matters. It is a simple genealogical mention, indicating that Ishmael was a man of influence whose son held an important position at the royal court.

sens: Son of Abraham and Hagar, ancestor of the Arab peoples
Military leader who helped the priest Jehoiada restore King Joash
H3458K.detail:
1. Ishmael is first the son that Abraham had with Hagar, Sarah's servant. According to Genesis, God chose him and promised that many nations would come from him. His name means "God will hear." He is presented as the father of the Arab peoples and received circumcision as a sign of the divine covenant.
2. In the provided usage (2 Chronicles 23:1), Ishmael is one of the military leaders of Judah who, in the seventh year of Joash's reign, joined the priest Jehoiada to overthrow the usurper Athaliah and restore the young king to the throne.
H3458K.origine: The name Ishmael literally means "God will hear" (from Shaddai, "Almighty God," and the verb "to hear"). It is a name that expresses the idea that God listens to prayer and answers the cry of the suffering one. Abraham recognizes in him the son that God had announced to him, even though he was not born of an explicit promise regarding the inheritance of salvation.
H3458K.emploi: Ishmael primarily appears as a major figure in the story of Abraham: a rejected son after the birth of Isaac, he is also the one through whom a divine promise of numerous descendants is fulfilled. He is notably mentioned in Genesis (his birth, his circumcision, his expulsion). In the New Testament, Paul cites Ishmael to illustrate the contrast between the flesh and the Spirit, between the promise and the law. The provided usage presents a different Ishmael: a military leader of Judah (2 Chronicles 23:1) who, under Joash's reign, played a political and military role alongside Jehoiada.
H3458K.portee: The story of Ishmael, son of Abraham, reminds the believer that God sees distress and promises help, even when the situation seems hopeless. It also teaches that the fulfillment of divine promises follows the path that God has laid out, not the one we imagine. For the Christian, it invites us to distinguish between what is born of our own effort and what truly arises from faith in God's promise.

sens: Priest from the family of Pashhur who had married a foreign woman
H3458L.detail: 1. Ishmael is a priest belonging to the priestly family of Pashhur, mentioned only once in the Bible during the time of the Exile and the return. Like other priests of his time, he had taken a foreign woman as his wife, which was contrary to the law of Israel. During the reforms led by Ezra, he had to repudiate this woman (Ezra 10:22).
H3458L.origine: The name Ishmael means "God will hear" or "God will listen," composed of the Hebrew verb "shama'" (to hear, to listen) and the divine name "El" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses confidence in divine action. The same name has been borne by several important characters in biblical history, including the son of Abraham and Hagar, but the one mentioned here in Ezra 10:22 is a simple priest from the time of the return from Exile.
H3458L.emploi: This character appears only once in the Scriptures, in Ezra 10:22. He is among the priests and Levites who had to send away their foreign wives during the spiritual reform led by Ezra after the return from Babylon. His appearance in this list shows that even the temple servants, upon returning from Exile, had committed this sin by marrying women from foreign nations. This episode illustrates the efforts to restore worship and the religious purity of Israel after the Exile.
H3458L.portee: This passage reminds us of the importance that the Bible places on the holiness of God's people and the separation from idolatrous practices. For today's believer, it is a call to take seriously the alliances we enter into, especially in areas where our faith is at stake. The mention of Ishmael shows that no one is exempt from this responsibility, not even priests and religious leaders.

sens: Descendant of Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar
Merchant or caravan trader from the Arabian desert
Member of an ancient Middle Eastern nomadic people
H3459.detail:
1. The Ishmaelites are the descendants of Ishmael, the son that Abraham had with his servant Hagar. Ishmael means "God will hear" in Hebrew. Cast out from Abraham's household with his mother, Ishmael became the father of a great lineage (twelve sons according to Genesis 25), founding the peoples of the Arabian desert. This genealogy fundamentally defines this people: to be an Ishmaelite is to be of Ishmael's blood.

2. In the Bible, the Ishmaelites primarily appear as merchants and traders. In Genesis 37:25, a "caravan of Ishmaelites" passes near Dothan carrying "spices, balm, and myrrh" to Egypt: they are traders who traverse the routes of ancient commerce. Joseph is sold to these merchants (Genesis 37:28) who then sell him to Potiphar in Egypt (Genesis 39:1).

3. In Judges 8:24, Gideon observes that the defeated enemies "had gold rings, for they were Ishmaelites": this evokes the wealth and prestige of these nomadic desert peoples, known for their possessions and power. The Ishmaelites thus also embody political and economic power in the ancient world.
H3459.origine: The word "Ishmaelite" comes from the proper name Ishmael (יִשְׁמָעֵאל) which literally means "God will hear." Ishmael was the son that Abraham had with Hagar, Sarai's Egyptian servant, before the birth of Isaac. Although cast out from Abraham's house in obedience to God, Ishmael received from God the promise that "a great nation would come from him" (Genesis 21:13, 18). The suffix "-ite" in Hebrew (כִּי, formed from יִשְׁמָעֵאלִי) designates members of the same clan or people, those who descend from a common ancestor. The Ishmaelites were known as desert peoples, excelling in trade and herding.
H3459.emploi: The word "Ishmaelite" or "Ishmaelites" appears 8 times in the Segond, mainly in the account of Joseph in Genesis 37-39. Joseph's brothers, jealous of him, decide to sell him; they first propose to sell him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:27), and then the deal is actually concluded with them (Genesis 37:28 and 39:1). This Ishmaelite trade changes Joseph's destiny and leads him to Egypt. In Judges 8:24, the term refers to the military enemies defeated by Gideon, recognizable by their gold rings. In 1 Chronicles 2:17 and 27:30, we find Ishmaelite individuals integrated into the life of Israel. The word thus describes a people with varied activities: trade, herding, and relations with Israel.
H3459.portee: The Ishmaelites remind believers that God keeps His promises even to those who are excluded from the main covenant. Ishmael, rejected from Abraham's house, nevertheless received a blessing and a numerous offspring. For the modern reader, the Ishmaelites also embody the providential role of divine Providence: the sale of Joseph to the Ishmaelite merchants, an act of malice by his brothers, becomes the instrument by which God places him in Egypt to later save his family from famine. What seems like misfortune becomes grace.

sens: Warrior from Gibeon in the service of King David
Leader of thirty soldiers among David's mighty men
H3460G.detail:
1. Ishmaiah is a man from Gibeon (an important city of Benjamin) who rallied to David and served among his mightiest warriors. He appears in the list of elite soldiers who came to support him at Ziklag, before he became king (1 Chronicles 12:4).
2. He held a military responsibility: leader of the thirty, meaning commander of a unit of thirty warriors in David's army. This rank shows that he was both a formidable fighter and a respected officer.
H3460G.origine: The name Ishmaiah means in Hebrew "God hears" or "Yahweh hears": it combines the idea of a prayer heard by the Lord. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name, which was common among the Israelites to express their faith and trust in God.
H3460G.emploi: Ishmaiah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:4. He is listed among the powerful warriors who rallied to David at Ziklag, before he took the throne. This list enumerates the men who came to support him during his flight from Saul. Ishmaiah is noted as a renowned Gibeonite, highlighting that even non-Levitical cities provided valuable fighters to the king.
H3460G.portee: The role of Ishmaiah reminds us that service to the king of God attracts men from all backgrounds, including non-Israelites or men from small towns. His name, which means "God hears," is an invitation to remember that God listens to those who serve Him faithfully and places them alongside His chosen ones.

sens: Gibeonite warrior in the service of King David
Leader of the tribe of Zebulun under David's reign
H3460H.detail:
1. Jishmaiah is a Gibeonite — originally from Gibeon — who distinguished himself as one of the mightiest warriors in the service of King David (1 Chronicles 27:19). He is one of those courageous men who formed the core of the royal army at the time when David was consolidating his power.
2. Under David's reign, Jishmaiah was appointed as chief (or governor) of the tribe of Zebulun, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. His name appears in the official list of tribal leaders established by the king, showing the trust that David placed in him to lead his people.
H3460H.origine: His name means "Yahweh will hear" or "God will hear." It is formed from the Hebrew "Yish" ("he") and "Shema" ("to hear") combined with the divine name "Yah." It is a name of trust, common among the faithful of Israel, expressing the hope that the Lord listens to the prayers of those who call upon Him.
H3460H.emploi: Jishmaiah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:19, where he is mentioned in the list of tribal chiefs appointed by King David. He is presented as the son of Obadiah and as responsible for Zebulun. This unique mention, although brief, places him at the heart of the administrative and military system of the united kingdom under David, alongside other tribal leaders tasked with governing their peoples and contributing to the defense of the kingdom.

sens: A man of the tribe of Benjamin
H3461.detail: Jishmerai is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the division of the kingdom between Israel and Judah. He is the son of Elpaal and the brother of several other Benjamites, including Jobab, Eber, and Meshullam. He belongs to an important family of this tribe, but the Bible reports nothing else about his life or actions.
H3461.origine: The name Jishmerai literally means "He keeps me" or "The one who keeps me." It is composed of the Hebrew root "shamar" (to keep, observe, protect) and a personal element. This name expresses trust in divine protection, a common intention in ancient Hebrew names. The family of Elpaal to which he belongs is well-known in the Benjamite genealogies.
H3461.emploi: Jishmerai appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:18, where he is listed among the sons of Elpaal in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is part of a long list of descendants that served to establish and document the family ties of the tribes after the Babylonian exile. His name appears alongside that of his brother Jobab, also a son of Elpaal. No event or action is attached to him: he is known only by his genealogy.

sens: To fall asleep, to be asleep, to rest in sleep
To remain for a long time, to be kept for a long time (for a harvest or a good)
To be inactive, to slumber, to neglect to do something
H3462.detail:
1. Sleep simply means to fall asleep or to be in a state of sleep: the body rests, the mind stops. This is what Elijah does in 1 Kings 19:5 when he lies down and falls asleep under a broom tree, or what the man does in Genesis 2:21 when God puts him into a deep sleep. It is also the action of resting in trust, as the psalmist expresses in Psalms 4:9: "I lie down and sleep in peace."
2. Sleep can also mean to remain for a long time in a state of preservation or inactivity: an old harvest that "sleeps" in the granaries before being consumed, as in Leviticus 26:10, where God promises that you will eat "old harvests." It is the image of something set aside that persists.
3. Sleep in a figurative sense means to be inactive, to slumber, to close one's eyes to something: when one "sleeps," one does not see, one does not react. The psalmist asks God in Psalms 44:24: "Why do you hide your face?" fearing that God might "sleep" and abandon Israel, while in Psalms 121:4 it is a comforting promise: "He who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep."
H3462.origine: The word יָשֵׁן comes from a root that denotes the state of rest of sleep. In Hebrew, it is the natural image of the body ceasing its activity. The root is also used to express anything that lasts a long time or accumulates (like a stored harvest), by extension of the idea that sleep is a form of pause or preservation. The word belongs to the family of states of the body and soul.
H3462.emploi: This word appears about twenty times in the Hebrew Bible. It primarily denotes ordinary, physical sleep: Elijah sleeps, Jacob dreams while sleeping (Genesis 41:5), Samson falls asleep on the knees of Delilah (Judges 16:19). In the Psalms, sleep takes on a spiritual hue: it is a sign of trust in God (Psalms 3:6, 4:9), or conversely, it is something God never does, for He watches over His people (Psalms 121:4). Among the prophets, sleep takes on a moral sense: it is inactivity, a lack of vigilance against evil (Isaiah 5:27 speaks of warriors who do not sleep from fatigue). The word is also used for things: an old harvest that persists for a long time (Leviticus 26:10), a lingering skin disease (Leviticus 13:11).
H3462.portee: This word teaches us several essential truths: sleep is a gift that God gives to those who fear Him, a legitimate rest in trust; God Himself never sleeps and constantly watches over His own; and in moral life, not sleeping means remaining vigilant, guarding one's soul and the commandments of God. For a believer, "sleeping in peace" becomes an image of the security found in God alone.

sens: to be in sleep, unconscious and motionless
to slumber, to be plunged into a deep sleep
to be inactive, asleep, ignorant
H3463.detail:
1. To be in sleep, unconscious and motionless: the word describes the physical state of one who sleeps deeply. In 1 Samuel 26:7, Saul is lying down and sleeping in the midst of his camp, unaware of what surrounds him. This is the natural sleep of the body that needs rest.
2. To slumber, to be plunged into a deep sleep: this sense emphasizes not only that one sleeps, but that one sleeps so deeply that one cannot see or hear. When David and Abishai come at night, "they were all sleeping a deep sleep" (1 Samuel 26:12), sent into this state by God Himself.
3. To be inactive, asleep, or ignorant, in a figurative sense: to sleep can mean to be detached, inattentive, or without action. In 1 Kings 18:27, Elijah mocks the god Baal by saying: "Perhaps he is sleeping," meaning that he is not paying attention to his worshipers. In Psalm 78:65, the Lord "awoke as one who has slept," an image of one who wakes up and resumes action.
H3463.origine: The Hebrew word ישׁן (yashen) comes from an ancient root that paints the image of rest and inactivity of the sleeping body. In the family of Hebrew words, it always denotes this state of unconsciousness or inaction. The image is that of sleep as a sort of temporary forgetfulness of the waking world.
H3463.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (1 Samuel, 1 Kings) and the poetic books (Psalms, Song of Solomon). In 1 Samuel 26, it describes Saul's natural and deep sleep, a sleep protected by God to allow David to act. In 1 Kings 3:20 and 18:27, it is again ordinary sleep or figurative inattentiveness. In Psalms 78:65, the Lord's awakening contrasts with a previous sleep. In Song of Solomon 5:2, the young girl is asleep but her heart remains awake, an image of love that does not sleep.
H3463.portee: This word teaches that sleep is a natural need and a gift from God, but it also invites one to be spiritually alert. Physically sleeping is good and orderly, but in figurative passages, being "asleep" spiritually — inattentive to the voice of God or to that of the one you love — is a danger. The Lord, however, never sleeps: He always watches over His people.

sens: Man living during the time of the united monarchy in Israel
H3464.detail: Jashen is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of mighty warriors of King David. His name literally means "sleeper" or "one who sleeps" in Hebrew. He is the father of at least one of David's valiant warriors: Jonathan, son of Jashen, is listed among the thirty warriors of the king (2 Samuel 23:32). This man is also known by the name Hashem, according to the parallel in the book of Chronicles.
H3464.origine: The name Jashen comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to sleep" or "to be asleep." It is a descriptive name, probably given for a reason related to sleep, although the Bible does not explain its origin. The same man is called "Hashem" ("the name") in 1 Chronicles 11:34, which may be a spelling variation or a nickname.
H3464.emploi: Jashen appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:32, in the list of David's thirty warriors. He is mentioned as the father of Jonathan, one of these valiant fighters. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 11:34 refers to him as Hashem, showing that both names refer to the same character in the royal record lists.

sens: Having advanced age, having existed for a long time
Ancient, long established
Having lost its novelty, its luster
H3465G.detail:
1. The word describes what has advanced age or has existed for a long time: it is the opposite of "new" or "young." In Nehemiah 3:6, the "old gate" is an ancient gate of Jerusalem, likely damaged by time and destruction, that the workers must restore.
2. This meaning extends to what is obsolete or worn out: an old thing has lost its initial function or appeal. Here, the old gate needs to be repaired, covered, and its leaves, locks, and bars must be reinstalled — it can no longer stand on its own.
3. The word can also refer to the character of what belongs to the past, to a bygone era, as opposed to what is contemporary or modern.
H3465G.origine: The Hebrew word יָשָׁן (yashan) belongs to a small family of words meaning "ancient" or "old." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of elapsed time: what is old has had time to become so. The word fundamentally designates what has lived, what has endured, and which bears the marks of that duration. It is a simple and common word in biblical Hebrew for speaking of age or antiquity.
H3465G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:6, where it qualifies a gate of Jerusalem. This context of rebuilding the walls and gates of the city after the exile shows the importance of restoring the old structures: the old gates must be repaired, restored, and reinforced. The word emphasizes the damaged or worn character of what must be restored, making its use particularly relevant in a passage dealing with the reconstruction of a ruined city.
H3465G.portee: This word reminds us that old things can lose their function and solidity, but they are worth restoring and renewing. In the context of Nehemiah, it illustrates the patient work of rebuilding after a period of destruction: what was old and damaged regains life and utility. For the Christian reader, it also speaks of renewal and restoration — God can make solid and beautiful what was old and in ruins.

sens: Dating back a long time, existing for a long time
Produced or preserved prior to another
Relating to a bygone era
H3465H.detail:
1. This word designates what is old, which has existed for a long time or dates back to a distant time. In Leviticus 25:22, the "ancient" harvest is that of the previous year, preserved and consumed before the new harvest.
2. It applies to what has been produced before, to what was there before another thing came to replace it. In Leviticus 26:10, the "old" harvests must be brought out to make way for the new, which implies regular storage and renewal.
3. It qualifies a bygone time, an earlier era. In Song of Solomon 7:14, the lover says he has kept both "new and old" fruits — not out of lack, but out of deliberate affection, keeping in reserve what was old alongside the new.
H3465H.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of old age and the preservation of things. It naturally opposes what is new and fresh. The primary notion is that of duration, of what has subsisted and persists, often with the underlying idea of reserve or deposit — hence the biblical notion of storage and preservation.
H3465H.emploi: The word appears four times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the laws of Leviticus concerning the sabbatical years (Leviticus 25:22 and 26:10), where it describes the old harvests preserved from one year to the next. These verses emphasize divine provision: God promises such an abundant harvest in the sixth year that one will eat from old stores until the ninth year. The word also appears in the Song of Solomon (7:14) where the old fruits kept show faithful love, and in Isaiah 22:11 for the "ancient" pool, a water reservoir established long ago.
H3465H.portee: This word reminds us of God's faithful provision: He ensures such a generous supply that one can keep the old while receiving the new. It also evokes the wisdom of storing up and not wasting anything. For the believer, it invites one to see God's hand in regular abundance and to trust the one who knows how to prepare for the future from afar.

sens: Fortified city of the Northern Kingdom, near Bethel
H3466G.detail: Jeshana is a city located at the southern border of the Northern Kingdom, not far from Bethel. It appears in the account of the war between Abijah, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel (2 Chronicles 13:19). The name likely means "reserve" or "storehouse," perhaps evoking a place where provisions were stored. During this military campaign, Abijah conquers Jeshana as well as several other cities with their surrounding territories, demonstrating its strategic importance as a fortified point in the north.
H3466G.origine: The Hebrew name יְשָׁנָה (Jeshana) probably derives from a root meaning "old" or "reserve." It is a toponym, that is, a place name, typical of the geography of ancient Levant. The city owes its existence to its strategic position and its probable role in controlling the territory and trade routes of northern Israel.
H3466G.emploi: Jeshana appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 13:19. It is mentioned in the context of Abijah's victorious military campaign against Jeroboam, king of the separatist Northern Kingdom. The city is listed among a group of conquered localities (Bethel, Ephron, and their territories), indicating that it was significant enough to be explicitly named during this victory. Its location near Bethel, a major religious center of the North, underscores its geopolitical importance.

sens: Gate of the city of Yeshanah, located near Bethel at the southern border of the Northern Kingdom
H3466H.detail: Yeshanah is a city gate mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:39, in the context of the consecration of the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. The name means "ancient" or "old" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a structure or place of antiquity. This gate was located near Bethel, at the southern border of the Northern Kingdom, and marked a strategic point in biblical geography.
H3466H.origine: The name Yeshanah derives from the Hebrew root yashén (יָשָׁן) which means "old" or "ancient." This root expresses the idea of antiquity or what has lasted a long time. The word appears in other biblical contexts to designate what is worn by time or established for a long time. Here, the name of the gate or city carries the idea of something ancient, likely due to its history or character as an old structure.
H3466H.emploi: Yeshanah appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:39, during the account of the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from Babylonian exile. It is mentioned as a landmark during the processional route around the city. Although geographically associated with the Northern Kingdom, near Bethel, this reference appears in a post-exilic context centered on Jerusalem, making it a geographical reference point in the reconstituted geography of Israel.

sens: Deliver someone from danger or an enemy, allowing them to escape
Grant victory in battle, protect against an adversary
Rescue someone who cries for help
Free from guilt or moral sin
Preserve, protect from destruction or perdition
H3467.detail:
1. Deliver someone from danger or an enemy: this means pulling someone from a situation where they risk death or misfortune. Exodus 2:17 shows Moses defending the shepherd's daughters against stronger men — he saves them from immediate danger.
2. Grant victory in battle: this means making someone triumph over their adversaries. 1 Samuel 14:6 asks if God can "save" by few or by many, meaning to grant victory regardless of the strength of the danger.
3. Rescue someone who cries for help: this means responding to the call of someone in distress. Psalms 55:17 expresses this confidence: "I cry out to God, and the Lord will save me" — He will hear and intervene.
4. Free from guilt or sin: this means purifying the soul from the evil that stains it. Jeremiah 4:14 calls to purify from evil "so that you may be saved," which here means to be preserved from condemnation.
5. Preserve from destruction: this means keeping alive and protecting life. This can concern both a battle and a disease, a famine, or any threat to existence.
H3467.origine: This verb comes from the root ysh, which expresses the idea of widening, freeing space, making room — hence the idea of coming out of narrowness, danger, or prison. The noun yeshuah (salvation, deliverance) derives directly from it, as does the proper name Yeshoua (Jesus), "God saves." This root is also found in the names Hosea ("God saves") and Joshua ("God saves"), which remind us of the heart of the ministry of these men of God: to save and liberate the people.
H3467.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament, used 199 times. It appears mainly in war narratives (Judges, Samuel, Kings), where God "saves" Israel from its enemies and from servitude: He saves through judges (Judges 2:16), through kings (1 Samuel 9:16), through superhuman acts (1 Samuel 14:6). It is also used in the psalms as a cry of confidence towards God in the face of moral or spiritual danger (Psalms 6:5, 7:2). In Proverbs and Job, it takes on a more internal meaning: saving from sin (Proverbs 20:22), helping the poor. The two forms of the verb are distinguished: the passive form ("to be saved") emphasizes the deliverance received, while the active form ("to save") highlights the action of the one who saves, often God.
H3467.portee: This word reveals that the God of Israel is not distant: He saves, He intervenes, He hears the cry of those who plead with Him. For the believer, "to save" is not just a distant judicial act, but a living action, here and now, in the face of suffering, guilt, and oppression. This underpins prayer and hope: one can cry out to God as in Psalm 55:17, assured that He will come to our aid. This word also sheds light on why Jesus bears the name Yeshoua: He comes to save, fulfilling God's mission since the Exodus.

sens: Deliverance from immediate danger or threat
Security, protection, lasting well-being
Victory won by God
Prosperity and success granted by God
The complete work of God to save His people
H3468.detail:
1. Deliverance from danger: when one escapes a peril that threatens, like a soldier who comes out alive from a battle. David speaks of God: "You are my shield against violence" (2 Samuel 22:3), this is that immediate deliverance from evil.

2. Security and well-being: the tranquil state that follows when one is safe and prospering. The word denotes both the rescue and the peace it brings: the one who has found their "salvation" lives without fear, like David who cries, "Come, let us sing for joy to the Rock of our salvation" (Psalms 95:1), celebrating the stability that God gives him.

3. Victory of God: when the Lord Himself achieves success against the enemies of His people, like a warrior who wins the battle. This salvation comes from God alone, not from our strength.

4. Granted prosperity: the material and moral well-being that God spreads, like the absence of misfortune for the children of a virtuous man (Job 5:4).

5. The sovereign action of God: salvation is not primarily a feeling, but the active intervention of God who restores His people (Isaiah 45:8: "Let justice flow down from the heavens").
H3468.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be wide, spacious, liberated." Salvation evokes the idea of coming out of a narrow or confined space (danger, slavery) to enter a free and safe space. That is why it designates both the deliverance itself and the regained freedom. The family of this word also includes the noun "width" and the adjective "just, victorious." In biblical Hebrew, salvation is always the work of God towards the one in need.
H3468.emploi: This word appears 35 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and among the prophets. It first describes concrete deliverance: David cries out to God to save him from his enemies. But gradually, salvation expands: it denotes the well-being of the entire people, the prosperity granted by the Lord, and ultimately the hope of a definitive intervention from God. The psalmists speak of "God of my salvation" (Psalms 27:9, Psalms 62:8), placing salvation at the heart of the personal relationship with the Lord. The prophets announce that salvation will come for all peoples (Isaiah 51:5, Isaiah 62:11). This word lays the foundation for the entire biblical theology of salvation: only God saves.
H3468.portee: For today's believer, this word reminds us that salvation is never our work, but that of God alone. It is not primarily a feeling of inner well-being, but a real deliverance and a restored relationship with God. Biblical salvation is rooted in trust: this is why the psalmists "cry" out to God and do so with joy. It invites the reader to recognize their dependence on God and to celebrate His intervention for them.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H3469G.detail: Ischei is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of the house of Hezron. He is the son of Appaim and the father of Sheshan, placing him in the lineage of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:31).
H3469G.origine: The name Ischei means "He saves me" in Hebrew, composed of the root for "to save" and the pronoun "me." It is a theophoric name (bearing the divine name) that expresses trust in divine deliverance.
H3469G.emploi: Ischei appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:31, in the genealogy of the descendants of Jerahmeel. It is a simple genealogical mention that places him in the succession of generations of Judah, without a detailed account of his life. The Segond transliterates it as "Jischeï."

sens: A chief of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
A descendant of Judah in the genealogy of Hezron
H3469H.detail:
1. Jischeï is a man of the people of Judah who lived during the period when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two: the Northern Kingdom (Israel) and the Southern Kingdom (Judah). He is mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 4:20, where he appears as the head of a family and the father of two sons: Zocheth and Ben-Zocheth.
2. He is part of the genealogical lineage of Judah that traces back to Hezron, the founding ancestor of an important branch of this tribe. The Bible lists the family heads and the generations that have perpetuated the people of Judah through the centuries.
H3469H.origine: The name Jischeï means "He saves me" in Hebrew. It is formed from the root yasha, which expresses the idea of saving, delivering, and the personal pronoun "me." This name reflects the father's trust in divine deliverance. Several men bore this name in ancient Israel, including a chief of Manasseh and a chief of Simeon, but this one is particularly identified by his genealogical context.
H3469H.emploi: Jischeï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:20. This passage is part of a detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah, where the author lists the families and their heads. Jischeï is presented as the father of Zocheth and Ben-Zocheth, indicating that he was a recognized family leader in the official genealogy of Judah. His sole mention shows that he was a secondary figure, important mainly for his place in the genealogical succession of Israel.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H3469I.detail: Jischeï is a leader of the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible. He lived at a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two separate kingdoms. He is known as the father of four sons — Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel — who led a military expedition of five hundred men from Simeon to the mountain of Seir to fight (1 Chronicles 4:42).
H3469I.origine: The name Jischeï literally means "He saves me" or "My salvation," derived from the Hebrew root for "to save." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God or expresses a relationship with God, common in the Old Testament.
H3469I.emploi: Jischeï appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:42. He is mentioned in the context of a genealogical list of the children of Simeon, where the family heads and important figures of this tribe are enumerated. It is in this genealogy that we learn he was the father of four sons who distinguished themselves by a notable military action: the conquest of lands at the mountain of Seir, in the southern territory of Edom.

sens: Leader of Manasseh son of Appaim, of the lineage of Jerahmeel
H3469J.detail: Jischeï is a figure from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the genealogy of the northern tribes. He appears in 1 Chronicles 5:24 among the leaders of their fathers' houses, presented as a valiant man and a renowned chief. His name means "He saves me" in Hebrew, which evokes trust in divine deliverance. Although little known, he represents those leaders of Manasseh who maintained order and family responsibility during the time of the divided monarchy.
H3469J.origine: The name Jischeï comes from Hebrew and literally means "He saves me" or "My savior." This root expresses trust in divine deliverance and protection. The name reflects the faith of the one who received it or of his parents in God's saving action. It is a theophoric name, affirming a spiritual dimension of the life of the bearer.
H3469J.emploi: Jischeï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:24. The passage lists the leaders of Manasseh who lived during the time of the divided monarchy. We learn that he was the son of Appaim and belonged to the lineage of Jerahmeel, from the house of Hezron. He is described as a valiant man and a renowned chief among the leaders of his tribe living east of the Jordan. This unique mention shows his importance in tribal organization, even though no details about his deeds are reported.

sens: Great prophet of Judah in the 8th century B.C.
Son of Amoz, father of Shear-Jashub and Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz
Author of the prophetic book that bears his name
H3470A.detail: 1. Isaiah is the great prophet who lived during the time of the kings of Judah Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (8th century B.C.). He regularly intervenes with King Hezekiah to convey the words of the Lord, especially during the threat from the Assyrian king Sennacherib (Isaiah 37:21). 2. He is the son of Amoz and the father of two sons with symbolic names: Shear-Jashub ("a remnant will return") and Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz ("the spoil speeds, the prey hastens"), which embody the prophet's message of judgment and deliverance. 3. Isaiah composed the prophetic book that bears his name, a masterwork of biblical revelation, gathering his visions and words (Isaiah 1:1; 2 Chronicles 32:32).
H3470A.origine: The name Isaiah means "Jehovah (the Lord) has saved" or "the Lord is my salvation." It expresses the essence of Isaiah's prophetic message: the Lord remains the savior of His people, even in times of political crisis. This name anchors the prophet's mission in the assurance of divine salvation.
H3470A.emploi: Isaiah appears 32 times in the Bible, primarily in Kings and Chronicles for accounts of his life, and in his own book. In Kings (chapters 19-20), he is presented as the spiritual advisor to King Hezekiah in the face of the Assyrian crisis: he receives words from the Lord and conveys them to the king (2 Kings 19:2; 20:4). In the book of Isaiah itself (chapters 1, 7, 20, 37-39), he reports his visions and executes the Lord's commands, including symbolic acts (Isaiah 20:2). Rabbinic tradition states that he was martyred under King Manasseh.
H3470A.portee: Isaiah embodies the faithfulness of the prophet who boldly conveys the word of the Lord, even in times of political danger. His ministry shows that the God of Israel remains sovereign over history and a source of salvation for His people. The study of his life and teachings nourishes the believer's faith in the sovereignty and goodness of the Lord.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Son of Hananiah and brother of Pelatiah
Descendant of Zerubbabel
H3470B.detail: Isaiah is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, but this one specifically refers to a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 3:21. He is the son of Hananiah and the brother of Pelatiah, Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah, and Shecaniah. Through his genealogy, he is the great-grandson of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the return from exile and the reconstruction of the temple. His name, although borne by several characters in the Bible, means "the Lord has saved" and reflects trust in divine intervention.
H3470B.origine: The name Isaiah comes from the Hebrew Yeshayahu, composed of two elements: "Yah" (short form of the divine name the Lord) and "shaa" (to save, to deliver). It literally means "the Lord has saved" or "the Lord is salvation." This name was borne by several characters in biblical genealogies, particularly after the exile, expressing hope in divine deliverance.
H3470B.emploi: This character is known only by his mention in 1 Chronicles 3:21, in the genealogy of the royal descent of Judah. He appears in the list of the sons of Hananiah, himself the son of Shecaniah, grandson of Zerubbabel. This genealogy enumerates the descendants of Zerubbabel after the return from exile, showing how the royal lineage was perpetuated among the returned exiles. There are no other details about his life or deeds.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi during the time of the divided monarchy
Son of Rechabiah and father of Joram
H3470G.detail:
1. Isaiah is a man of the tribe of Levi mentioned during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between north and south. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of the priest Eleazar.
2. In the genealogical lineage reported in 1 Chronicles 26:25, Isaiah is the son of Rechabiah and the father of Joram: he occupies a place in this chain of transmission that shows how the responsibilities of the temple were passed down from generation to generation among the Levites.
H3470G.origine: The name "Isaiah" literally means "Jehovah has saved" or "God saves." It comes from two Hebrew words: a form of the verb "to save" and the name of God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God and expresses a conviction of faith in divine protection. Several people bore this name in ancient Israel.
H3470G.emploi: Isaiah is a Levite mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 26:25, in the context of a genealogical list detailing the descendants of Eleazar and their role in temple service. This passage shows that Levitical families maintained well-documented lines of service. Although this Isaiah is a simple link in this genealogy, his inclusion indicates that the temple and its services were organized according to hereditary family responsibilities.
H3470G.portee: This passage reminds us that every believer, even one whose name appears only once in the Bible, has a place in God's plan. Isaiah represents the generations of faithful who served in the temple without leaving behind great written exploits, but fulfilling their task with faithfulness. This speaks to anyone who wonders if their contribution to God's service has value when it goes unnoticed.

sens: Son of Jeduthun, Levitical musician during the united monarchy
H3470H.detail: 1. Isaiah is a son of Jeduthun, an important figure in the worship of the Jerusalem temple. His father Jeduthun was a musician and prophet who led a group of Levitical singers. Isaiah himself was part of these temple musicians, tasked with praising God through music and song (1 Chronicles 25:3). He had several brothers who also performed this sacred function before the Lord.
H3470H.origine: The Hebrew name Yeshayahu literally means "the Lord has saved." It is a theophoric name that expresses trust in divine deliverance. It was borne by several important men in Israel's history, notably the great prophet Isaiah (son of Amoz), but also by other figures, including this Levitical musician from the time of King David.
H3470H.emploi: This Isaiah appears twice in the first book of Chronicles, in chapter 25, which lists the temple musicians organized by David. He is first mentioned among the sons of Jeduthun (25:3), and then mentioned again in verse 15 as the leader of a group of twelve musicians assigned to the service of the temple. These two references indicate his role in the liturgical organization of Israelite worship, where the Levites had an essential responsibility.
H3470H.portee: This character reminds us that the service of the temple was not reserved for priests alone: the Levites, and particularly the musicians, played a central role in Israel's worship. The existence of such precise organization of singers and musicians shows the importance that the community placed on music in the praise of God.

sens: Man from the exile and return to Jerusalem
Son of Athaliah and leader of the house of Elam
Leader who returned with Ezra from captivity
H3470I.detail:
1. Isaiah is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return of the Hebrews from exile in Babylon at the time of Ezra. He is identified as the son of Athaliah and as the leader of the house of Elam, one of the families brought to Babylon (Ezra 8:7).
2. Leading a group of seventy men from his family, Isaiah is among those who decide to return to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple. He thus represents one of the great families participating in the restoration of Israel after the exile.
3. His name means "Jehovah has saved," reflecting his parents' faith in God's deliverance — a hope particularly significant for a child born during captivity or in such difficult times.
H3470I.origine: The name יְשַׁעְיָה (Isaiah) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to save" or "to deliver." It is composed of two elements: the divine name "Jah" (Jehovah) and the verb "to save." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, very common in Israel to express trust in divine protection. The same name is borne by other characters in the Old Testament.
H3470I.emploi: Isaiah appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:7, where Ezra establishes the list of family leaders who join him for the return journey from Babylon. He is presented as the son of Athaliah and leader of the house of Elam, with seventy men under his authority. This brief but honorable mention shows that he was a respected leader and a man of responsibility at the crucial moment of the return of the exiles. His inclusion in this list indicates his important role in the restoration of Jerusalem and its worship.

sens: Leader of the descendants of Merari who returned with Ezra after the Babylonian exile
H3470J.detail: 1. Isaiah is a Levitical leader from the house of Merari. He is among the leaders of families who accompanied Ezra during the return from the Babylonian exile, leading twenty of his brothers and their sons (Ezra 8:19). He is a representative of the religious and communal restoration of the people of Israel after captivity.
H3470J.origine: The Hebrew name means "Yahweh has saved," formed from the verb "to save" and the divine name. It is a common theophoric name in ancient Judaism, expressing trust in divine salvation. Several men bore this name around the time of the exile and return.
H3470J.emploi: Isaiah appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:19. He is mentioned as one of the leaders of the Levitical families who returned to Jerusalem with Ezra in the fifth century B.C. His role was to lead the descendants of Merari (a branch of the Levites) in this official migration for the reconstruction of the temple and the Jewish community. His inclusion in the list underscores the importance of the Levites' role in the post-exilic religious restoration.

sens: Man of Judah during the exile and return
Son of Hananias and brother of Pelatiah
Benjaminite mentioned in the list of inhabitants of Jerusalem
H3470K.detail: 1. Isaiah is a man who lived during the Babylonian exile and the return to Judah, in the generations following the destruction of the first temple. He belongs to an important family linked to Zerubbabel. 2. He is the son of Hananias and the brother of Pelatiah, himself the grandson of the governor Zerubbabel who led the return of the exiles. 3. In Nehemiah 11:7, Isaiah appears in the genealogy of a Benjaminite established in Jerusalem after the return from exile: he is an ancestor, through the line of his descendants, of whom Ithiel is named.
H3470K.origine: The name Isaiah (Hebrew Yeshayah) literally means "Jehovah has saved," formed from the Hebrew verb "to save" and the divine name. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, very common among the Hebrews. This name celebrates divine deliverance and expresses hope for God's salvation.
H3470K.emploi: Isaiah appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:7. He is cited as an ancestor of a Benjaminite whose name appears in the list of inhabitants of Jerusalem after the return from exile. This man is part of a genealogy that testifies to the reconstitution of the people of Judah after the Babylonian captivity, in the context of the return and reconstruction of the holy city.

sens: Precious stone of variable color, often red, yellow, or brown, used in jewelry and ornaments
Fine stone symbolizing beauty and wealth in liturgical or royal contexts
H3471.detail:
1. Jasper is a natural precious stone, opaque, with varied colors (red, yellow, brown), highly valued in antiquity for its beauty and durability. It appears in the account of the high priest's garment: it is featured in the fourth row of the breastplate, along with other magnificent gems, set in gold (Exodus 28:20 and 39:13).
2. Jasper symbolizes divine splendor and wealth when listed among the most precious stones. Ezekiel mentions it while describing the adornment of the king of Tyre, covered with fabulous stones: sardius, topaz, diamond, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, beryl, and emerald (Ezekiel 28:13). This enumeration evokes the brilliance and magnificence of one who was in Eden, the garden of God.
H3471.origine: The Hebrew word יָשְׁפְה comes from the Semitic root that designates this stone since ancient times. Jasper, a crystalline mineral from the quartz family, bears the same name in Greek (ἴασπις, iaspis) and in Latin (iaspis), showing the continuity of the term across ancient cultures. It is a common borrowing in the languages of the Near East, attested long before the Bible.
H3471.emploi: The word jasper appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of high value and prestige. Two occurrences are found in the details of the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28 and 39), where twelve precious stones symbolize the twelve tribes of Israel. The third occurrence is in a prophetic lament against the king of Tyre (Ezekiel 28), where jasper is named among the stones that adorned this prince before his fall. In all cases, jasper is never a trivial ornament: it marks luxury, divinity, or royal authority.
H3471.portee: For the believing reader, jasper reminds us that God reveres beauty and that this beauty, far from being superficial, reflects His glory. In the high priest's breastplate, each stone represents a tribe: jasper speaks of spiritual wealth entrusted by God to His people. In Ezekiel, its presence in the description of the fall of the king of Tyre invites us to see that all earthly splendor, even brilliant, does not escape God's judgment if pride corrupts it.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin
Son of Beria
Chief of a Benjaminite family
H3472.detail: Jischpha is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:16. He is presented as the son of Beria and the brother of several other men including Michael, Jocha, Arad, Ahio, and Shashak. He belonged to a family of tribal leaders, holding a position of responsibility among the Benjaminites during the time of the patriarchs.
H3472.origine: The name Jischpha literally means "He is bare" or "He is stripped," formed from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of nakedness or exposure. This type of theophoric name reveals a situation or a prayer of the parents at the time of birth, but its exact meaning eludes us today.
H3472.emploi: Jischpha is cited only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:16, where he appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. He is listed among the sons of Beria, alongside Michael and Jocha. This genealogical mention places him among the recognized heads of Benjaminite families in ancient Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Shashak
H3473.detail: Jischpan is a man belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Shashak and the brother of ten other children, including Eber, Eliel, Abdon, and Zichri. His name literally means "he hides" in Hebrew, but we know nothing of his life or actions beyond this genealogy.
H3473.origine: His Hebrew name יִשְׁפָּן comes from a root meaning "to hide" or "to conceal." He belongs to the genealogical line of Benjamin, recorded at the time of the division of the monarchy in Israel and Judah.
H3473.emploi: Jischpan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:22, in a genealogical list of men from the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy. He is presented solely by his lineage (son of Shashak) and his kinship with his brothers. This verse is part of a broader genealogy that lists the descendants of Benjamin, without specifying further details about Jischpan's life or role.

sens: Make straight, smooth, or level
Go straight, follow a direct path
Find good, judge suitable
Be just, straight, upright
Please, be agreeable
H3474.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to flatten, to make a surface smooth or straight. Isaiah 45:13 speaks of "flattening" the ways of Cyrus, as one flattens a path by removing obstacles. In sacred buildings, this verb was used to describe the smoothing and fitting of construction elements (1 Kings 6:35).

2. Figuratively, "to go straight" means to follow a path without detour, to progress directly. This evokes the image of the clear path that God prepares (Isaiah 40:3, Isaiah 45:2).

3. To find something "suitable" or "good": to judge that it is pleasing, that it is appropriate. When the assembly finds something "suitable" in 1 Chronicles 13:4, it means they approve the plan.

4. To be just and upright is to walk according to what is right. The psalmist finds all the ordinances of the Lord to be "just" (Psalms 119:128), recognizing that His Word is straight and true.

5. To be pleasing, to please: David's love "pleases" Michal (1 Samuel 18:20), it suits her and is agreeable to her.
H3474.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing primarily the physical idea of "straight" or "smooth." The same verb can take on figurative nuances: what is straight in the physical sense becomes "just" in the moral sense, what is smooth becomes "pleasant." The family includes words like "jashar" (straight, just) and "yashar" (uprightness). This evolution from the concrete to the figurative is typical of biblical thought: moral uprightness is experienced as a walk without detours.
H3474.emploi: The verb appears 25 times in the Hebrew Bible. In the literal sense of "to flatten" or "to smooth," it is mostly found in relation to constructions (temple, city) and in God's action of preparing paths (Isaiah 40, 45). In the sense of "to find good" or "to judge suitable," it appears in narratives (1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles) when a person or group approves a decision. In the moral sense of "to be just" or "upright," Psalms and Proverbs frequently use it: the righteousness of the just flattens his path (Proverbs 11:5), while the wicked takes crooked paths. The word thus plays on the image of a clear and straight path, which becomes a symbol of justice and pleasantness in the eyes of God.
H3474.portee: This word invites the believer to live in righteousness, knowing that God "flattens" the path of the just. It reminds that justice is not winding or crooked, but clear and direct. For one who walks straight according to the Word of God, the Lord Himself removes obstacles and makes his way straight and pleasant.

sens: Son of Caleb and grandson of Hezron in the genealogy of Judah
H3475.detail: 1. Jéscher is a man of the tribe of Judah, belonging to the family of Caleb. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Hezron, as the son of Caleb and his first wife Azubah (1 Chronicles 2:18). He is an ancestor of the people of Judah, whose name has been preserved in the genealogical record of Israel.
H3475.origine: The name Jéscher means "upright" or "correct" in Hebrew, formed from a root that evokes straightness and alignment. This name reflects a moral or physical quality valued in Hebrew culture. Jéscher belongs to the important genealogical line of Caleb, one of the great figures of the desert period, highlighting the significance of this family branch in the history of Israel.
H3475.emploi: Jéscher is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:18, in the context of the genealogical record of the descendants of Hezron. He is cited among the sons of Caleb born of Azubah, alongside Shobab and Ardon. This unique mention suggests that Jéscher did not play a major role in biblical history, but his presence in the genealogical record confirms his importance in the continuity of the lineage of Judah and the maintenance of the genealogy of God's people.

sens: quality of one who acts with justice and sincerity
moral correction and integrity of the heart
path or conduct in accordance with what is just
equity, what is due or appropriate
H3476.detail:
1. Uprightness primarily refers to the moral quality of one who is honest and just in their actions and words: it is to walk in the right path, without deceptive detours. When Job says, "I will speak with uprightness of heart" (Job 33:3), he means that he will speak with total sincerity, without lies or ulterior motives.
2. It also describes the internal integrity of the heart, a deep disposition to do good and to respect God. King David offers "in the uprightness of his heart" (1 Chronicles 29:17), which means that all his commitment comes from a sincere and pure will, not from a hypocritical appearance.
3. Uprightness is also the path, the moral way that the believer must follow. Abandoning "the paths of uprightness" (Proverbs 2:13) means leaving the way of justice to enter into the moral darkness of sin.
4. More broadly, it is what is due, appropriate, equitable according to divine law: this includes balance in actions, the refusal of excess (as in Proverbs 11:24).
H3476.origine: The Hebrew word יֹשֶׁר comes from a root that means "to be straight, linear" — the basic image is that of a line without curvature, without detour. From this arises the moral idea: a straight conduct is a conduct without detours, without cunning, without deviation towards evil. The word belongs to the lexical field of justice (צְדָקָה, tsedaqah) but emphasizes personal integrity and honesty more than conformity to an external law.
H3476.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Wisdom literature (Proverbs, Job, Psalms) and in the context of covenant. It describes the quality required of the faithful of the Lord: the uprightness of the heart is praised as a virtue that God loves (1 Chronicles 29:17), and the uprightness of the moral path is contrasted with the paths of darkness (Proverbs 2:13). In Deuteronomy (9:5), God clarifies that the entry into Canaan is not the result of the people's righteousness but of His sovereign grace. Uprightness also appears in the words of the righteous confronted with trial (Job 33:3): it is the adornment of one who wishes to plead their innocence before God with sincerity.
H3476.portee: For the Christian, uprightness reminds us that faith in God is not limited to the absence of external evil but requires integrity of heart: to think justly, to speak truthfully, to act without ulterior motives. It invites us to examine whether our commitment to God comes from a sincere will or mere appearance. It is also a call not to deviate from the path laid out by the Word, despite the temptations that push us towards darkness.

sens: That which is aligned, without curve or deviation
That which is in accordance with the law, with divine will
That which is just, equitable, correct in judgments
That which is honest, integral, without detour
That which is suitable, pleasing, appropriate
H3477G.detail:
1. The word first evokes a line or path without detours: "The path of the upright is to avoid evil" (Proverbs 16:17), like a straight way opposed to meanders.
2. In moral life, "right" means in accordance with the will of God: David "did what is right in the eyes of the Lord" (1 Kings 15:5), meaning he obeyed His commandments.
3. Applied to divine judgments and ordinances, the word expresses equity and justice: "You are righteous, O Lord! And Your judgments are equitable" (Psalms 119:137).
4. For a person, to be right is to be honest and sincere, without ulterior motives or duplicity: Job is described as "a blameless and upright man" (Job 1:1).
5. The word can also mean "that which is suitable" or "that which pleases": to do "what is right in the eyes of the Lord" (Exodus 15:26) means to do what pleases Him.
H3477G.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of extending straight, of being or going directly towards a goal. The basic image is that of a straight line, without curvature. In Hebrew, the same root gives "yashar" meaning "to make right," "to ensure victory," and "leader" or "prince." The word appears about 113 times in the Old Testament and applies to both physical paths and moral paths and divine justice.
H3477G.emploi: This word is one of the most important in the moral and religious vocabulary of the Old Testament. It appears 113 times, especially in the historical books (1 and 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles) when describing the behavior of kings: did they do what is right in the eyes of the Lord? It is also found intensely in the Psalms, which sing of God's uprightness and the blessed fate of the upright, and in Proverbs, which contrasts the right path with the twisted path of the wicked. In historical passages, "right" evaluates the king's faithfulness to the Law (Exodus 15:26: listening to God's voice and observing His commandments). In sapiential poetry, it expresses both personal moral integrity and the justice and uprightness of God Himself.
H3477G.portee: Understanding this word invites the Christian to see that living rightly is not a matter of appearance or external success, but of conformity to the revealed will of God. A right path, in the Bible, is a transparent and faithful path, without hypocritical detours. It is also an invitation to look to God as the supreme model of uprightness: His ordinances, His judgments are always right, and whoever follows Him walks on a good path.

sens: sacred book containing ancient stories and poems of Israel
H3477H.detail: 1. The "Book of the Just" is an ancient collection of important stories and poems for Israel, cited twice in the Bible. Its name literally means "of the just" or "of the right," perhaps because it contained texts celebrating the just and right deeds of the people. In Joshua 10:13, it describes the day when the sun stood still during the battle against the Amorites. In 2 Samuel 1:18, the song of the bow — David's lament over the death of Saul and Jonathan — is recorded there. This book has not come down to us intact, but the verses found in the Bible show us that it was a prestigious document, consulted to authenticate the great actions of Israel.
H3477H.origine: The Hebrew word means "just, right, uprightness." Its use as a book title suggests that it grouped together narratives deemed worthy, just, or conforming to the true history of Israel. It is unknown exactly when this book was compiled or lost.
H3477H.emploi: This title appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, solely in Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18. Both occurrences refer to the same ancient work, used as an authoritative source to record major events: the miracle of the sun standing still and a royal lament. The Bible does not describe the complete content of the Book of the Just, but these two citations show that it grouped poetic texts and historical narratives considered authentic and important for the memory of Israel.
H3477H.portee: This forgotten book reminds us that the Bible is not the only ancient text that Israel possessed. It also shows us that sacred authors cited other sources to strengthen the credibility of extraordinary narratives, such as the stopping of the sun. This invites the reader to reflect on how the Word of God was inscribed in the real history of Israel and how it relied on recognized testimonies.

sens: That goes in a straight line, without detour, without curve.
That is flawless, regular, well-proportioned in its structure.
That is just, fair, in accordance with what is good and proper.
That is honest, upright, faithful to the principles of justice and righteousness.
H3477I.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, "right" refers to what is straight, progressing in a direct line: it is the opposite of curved or twisted. In Jeremiah 31:9, the "smooth" path by which God leads the exiles is a path where the feet do not stumble, smooth and direct.
2. Applied to a physical structure or arrangement, "right" means well-aligned, regular, not leaning to the right or left. In Ezekiel 1:23, the wings of the creatures are "right" against each other, meaning parallel and well-fitted.
3. In a moral sense, "right" describes what is just, appropriate, in accordance with the order that God has established. In Ezra 8:21, a "happy" journey is literally a right journey, prosperous, without deviation from God's plan.
