4. Finally, "right" characterizes one who acts with righteousness, who does not deviate from just principles. In Micah 3:9, the leaders who "pervert all that is right" abandon justice itself; the word evokes a moral integrity that cannot be twisted.
H3477I.origine: The Hebrew word יָשָׁר (yashar) comes from a root that literally means "to go straight, to be in line." The same root gives rise to other words in the family of right and righteousness. It is a very concrete word at its core: in nature, what is straight — a road, an arrow, a tree — stands in opposition to what is twisted or curved. From there, the metaphor naturally extends to the moral realm: a "right" person is one who does not deviate, who goes straight in their actions and words, just like a well-marked path.
H3477I.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the provided usages, in very varied contexts. First in the physical realm: the wings of the cherubim are "right" (Ezekiel), and God leads His people by "smooth" paths (Jeremiah). Then in the realm of well-being and providence: a "happy" journey is a right journey, without obstacles (Ezra). Finally, in the moral and judicial realm: justice itself is what is "right," and those who "pervert" it bend it (Micah). The word thus glides from the physical image to the moral image, as if God invites His people to see ethical righteousness under the image of a straight and unwavering line.
H3477I.portee: For the Christian reader, this word right speaks of integrity: that of God first, who leads His children by a smooth path, without unnecessary detours; that which we are called to seek in our own actions and judgments. It is also an invitation to trust: to walk on a right path is to move forward without stumbling, knowing that one is not lost. God's justice is not a twisted or hidden justice; it is simple, transparent, right.

sens: The new name given to Jacob after his struggle with the angel at Peniel
The people and nation descended from Jacob
The northern kingdom after the division, composed of the ten tribes
The people of God as a whole, object of the covenant and the promise
H3478.detail:
1. Israel is the name that God gives to Jacob after his mysterious struggle with an angel near Peniel. This name means "God prevails" or "he who has struggled with God." It is a turning point in Jacob's life: his former name, which evoked cunning and deceit, is replaced by a name that celebrates his perseverance and desire to receive God's blessing (Genesis 32:28).
2. From Jacob's descendants, Israel becomes the name of the entire people that God formed and freed from Egypt. The "children of Israel" are the members of this people, bound together by a common genealogy and a covenant with the Lord. From the Exodus onward, this name designates the community that God guides and protects (Exodus 1:1-7).
3. After Solomon's death, the kingdom divides into two: the north becomes the kingdom of Israel (with ten tribes) under Jeroboam, while the south is named Judah (with two tribes). The name Israel then specifically applies to the northern kingdom (1 Kings 10:9).
4. Beyond these historical meanings, Israel designates in Scripture the people of the covenant, the one toward whom God's eternal love turns and to whom He has entrusted His promises and His Law.
H3478.origine: The name Israel comes from two Hebrew roots: "sarah" (to struggle, to persevere) and "El" (God). It literally means "he who has struggled with God" or "God prevails." This name is given after Jacob's struggle with the angel at Peniel, symbolizing a spiritual transformation and the strength received from God. The passage in Genesis 32:28 explains the meaning itself: "You have struggled with God and with men, and have prevailed."
H3478.emploi: The name Israel appears more than 2200 times in the Hebrew Bible. It first designates the patriarch Jacob renamed (Genesis 32:28, 35:10). Then it extends to his entire lineage: the children of Israel in Egypt (Exodus 1:1), the people freed by the Lord (Exodus 3:10-18), and the nation guided in the desert and established in Canaan. In the monarchical period, the term first applies to the unified kingdom (1 Kings 10:9), then to the northern kingdom after the division. After the exile, it encompasses the restored people. The name carries a theological dimension everywhere: Israel is the people of the covenant, the one whom God knows, loves, and protects.
H3478.portee: Understanding that the name Israel means "God prevails" profoundly illuminates the calling of this people: they were called not by their own strength, but by the power of God who chose and freed them. For today's believer, this story reminds us that God transforms names and destinies, and that true strength lies in relationship with God. The people of Israel also embodies the universal experience of one who seeks God's blessing and who, like Jacob, must learn to receive rather than to conquer through cunning.

sens: Jacob, the patriarch, called this by God after his struggle with the angel at Peniel
The people and nation of the descendants of Jacob
The northern kingdom after the division, formed of ten tribes
The people of God in general, throughout its history
H3479.detail:
1. Israel is the name of the one who was called Jacob before his miraculous encounter with God at Peniel (Genesis 32). In wrestling with the angel, Jacob showed a determination that pleased God, and he received this new name to mark this transformation and his new relationship with the Lord.
2. Israel also refers to all the descendants of Jacob — all the people descended from his twelve sons. It is the name of the people of God in a broad sense, the one that God had chosen and with whom He had made a covenant (Ezra 6:16: "The children of Israel, the priests and the Levites").
3. After the death of Solomon, the kingdom was divided into two: the south (Judah) and the north (Israel), which included ten tribes under the reign of Jeroboam. The term Israel can therefore refer specifically to this northern kingdom, distinct from Judah.
4. Generally, Israel remains the name of the entire people, even after the return from exile in Babylon: it is the people that God rebuilds and restores, as shown by the orders of the Persian kings for "all those of the people of Israel" to return to Jerusalem (Ezra 7:13).
H3479.origine: The name Israel means "God prevails" or "God rules" — it comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to struggle" or "to be strong." It is a name that evokes the strength and action of God, given as a reward to Jacob for his struggle of faith at Peniel. This name was then passed on to all his descendants, who carry in their very name the memory of the power of God that prevails over all things.
H3479.emploi: Israel appears in the texts of the Segond mainly in the books of Exodus, Kings, and the Prophets, and here in Ezra, which recounts the return of the people after the Babylonian exile. In these passages, Israel designates the entire people, recognized by foreign kings themselves as the people "of the God of heaven and earth" (Ezra 5:11). The term can refer to the historical nation (the people in its political and religious structures), to the assembled people (the children of Israel, the priests and the Levites gathered), or to those who descend from Israel in spirit. The context of Ezra shows it as the people that God restores and to whom He remains faithful despite captivity.
H3479.portee: For the Christian reader, Israel reminds us that God gives a new and divine meaning to the lives of those who seek Him and struggle with Him in faith — just as Jacob became Israel. It is also the name of the people that God has never abandoned, even in exile, which encourages the believer in trials. Finally, this people remains a sign of God's enduring covenant, and for Christians, Israel opens up to the mystery of God's plan that includes both Jews and Gentiles in His Church.

sens: Levite son of Asaph and chief musician of the temple
Chief of the seventh class of musicians during the divided monarchy
H3480.detail:
1. Jesarelah is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe dedicated to the service of the temple. He is the son of Asaph, a renowned musician and ancestor of a great dynasty of singers. In 1 Chronicles 25:14, he appears as the chief of the seventh class (or "course") of the temple musicians — those who shared the liturgical service in rotation.
2. His role was to lead a group of musicians (his "sons and brothers") responsible for playing instruments and singing during worship at the temple. This role of class leader was an important responsibility, as sacred music held a significant place in the worship of Israel.
H3480.origine: The name Jesarelah means "these are upright" or "this one is upright." He is also known by the name Asharelah (a variant of the same name). This Levite belongs to the lineage of Asaph, whose descendants formed one of the three great families of temple musicians according to the accounts in Chronicles.
H3480.emploi: Jesarelah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 25:14, where he is listed among the leaders of the twenty-four classes of musicians organized under King David. He is referred to as "the seventh," indicating that he led the seventh class. With his sons and brothers — twelve people in total — he was responsible for the musical service during the feasts and ceremonies at the temple.

sens: Descendant of Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar
Man living in the time of the Patriarchs, originally from Arabia
H3481G.detail:
1. An Ishmaelite is a man descended from Ishmael, born of the union of Abraham with his servant Hagar. Ishmael is the half-brother of Isaac and had twelve sons who founded Arab peoples: Nebajoth, Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Duma, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.

2. These Ishmaelites are men from the desert of Arabia, living in the time of the Patriarchs. In 2 Samuel 17:25, a certain Jithra, referred to as "the Israelite" in the text, is described as an Ishmaelite — probably a foreigner integrated into the Israelite community or a man of Ishmaelite origin who adopted the lifestyle of Israel.
H3481G.origine: The word comes from the name Ishmael (יִשְׁמָעֵאל), which means "God hears" (from שׁמע, "to hear," and אל, "God"). Ishmael is the son that Abraham had with Hagar, before the birth of Isaac. The term "Ishmaelite" thus designates any descendant of this patriarch and his lineage.
H3481G.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 17:25, where it qualifies Jithra, the father of Amasa who became general of Absalom's army. In this context, the term seems to designate a man of Ishmaelite origin who lived among the Israelites. Although the word is rare in biblical texts, the Ishmaelites as a people are regularly mentioned: they are the descendants of Ishmael and the Arab peoples that stem from them. They appear mainly in the genealogies of Genesis and in accounts of trade and contact with Israel.

sens: Descendant of Israel, the patriarch
Member of the people of Israel
Inhabitant of the kingdom of Israel
H3481H.detail:
1. An Israelite is primarily someone who descends from Israel, the patriarch whose name means "God prevails." Israel, also called Jacob, is the son of Isaac and the father of the twelve tribes that will form the people of Israel. In Leviticus 24:10, there is mention of a child whose "mother was an Israelite woman," showing that the term designates one who belongs to this lineage by heredity.
2. By extension, an Israelite is any member of the people of Israel, the religious and national community that God formed after the exodus from Egypt. It is the name that identifies them as the people of the covenant.
3. More broadly, the term applies to any inhabitant of the kingdom of Israel or to any person descended from this people, whether in the time of the patriarchs, of the monarchy, or of the exile.
H3481H.origine: The word comes from the proper name Israel (יִשְׂרָאֵל), which literally means "God prevails" or "the one who has struggled with God." This name was given to Jacob after a mysterious struggle with an angel at Peniel (Genesis 32:28). The descendants of Jacob thus receive the name Israelites because they descend from Israel and inherit the promise that God made to this patriarch.
H3481H.emploi: The word Israelite appears at least twice in the Hebrew Bible, notably in Leviticus 24:10-11, where it designates a person from this people. Although infrequent in the Old Testament written in Hebrew, the term becomes very common in Greek ("Israelite") to designate the members of the chosen people. It is used to identify someone by their belonging to this people, whether to evoke their genealogy, their religious status, or their rights in the community. Each Israelite shares the spiritual heritage of the patriarch Israel and is part of the covenant that God made with this people.
H3481H.portee: Understanding what an Israelite is helps the reader grasp the identity of the people that God has chosen and elected. It reminds us that the Christian Church, in the New Testament, is called the new Israel or spiritual Israel (see Galatians 6:16), highlighting the continuity between the people of the Old Covenant and the believers in Jesus Christ.

sens: quality of one who walks uprightly before God, without deviation or ulterior motives
integrity of heart, sincerity in the relationship with God
H3483.detail: 1. This word denotes moral uprightness, the quality of one who acts with justice and faithfulness toward God. In 1 Kings 3:6, Solomon praises his father David for having walked "in the uprightness of heart" — that is, with a sincere heart, without calculation or duplicity, seeking to please God. 2. Uprightness implies integrity: one does what is right not for show, but from the depth of the heart. It stands in opposition to hypocrisy and deceit. It is a mark of one who stands upright, honest and just, before the Lord.
H3483.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of straightness, of that which is upright and without curvature. Uprightness is thus the image of the straight path, applied to morality: one who walks in uprightness does not stray to the left or right, but moves directly toward good and toward God.
H3483.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 3:6. Solomon uses it to celebrate David's faithfulness: the deceased king walked "in the uprightness of heart toward God." This context shows that uprightness is the attitude of the just who seeks to obey God, who does not deceive Him and does not turn away from His commandments.
H3483.portee: This word reminds us that God values above all the sincerity of the heart. Uprightness is not an external performance, but an inner disposition of honesty and faithfulness toward God. It is a quality that the believer should desire for themselves: to walk in uprightness is to seek to please God not through hypocrisy, but through heartfelt obedience.

sens: Symbolic name for Israel designating the people in their ideal of uprightness
Chosen and beloved people of God, called to a just life
H3484.detail: 1. Yeshurun is a poetic name for Israel, used mainly in blessings and exhortations. The word literally means "the upright" or "the upright one," that is, one who stands upright, both physically and morally. In Deuteronomy 32:15, Moses uses this beautiful name just before reproaching Israel for its rebellion: "Israel grew fat and kicked" — the contrast shows that Yeshurun names who Israel should be, not who it has become. 2. This name also emphasizes that the people are the object of divine love and protection. In Isaiah 44:2, the Lord speaks to Yeshurun as to His chosen and formed servant, like a child whom He will care for. It is a title of honor and intimacy, not of condemnation.
H3484.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be upright" or "to be just." Yeshurun is a term of endearment, akin to saying "my little upright one" or "my upright one." It is a poetic nickname, created to express the moral and theological ideal of Israel, not a historical name. The connection with the people of Israel is that, in God's plan, they are called to live in uprightness and obedience.
H3484.emploi: Yeshurun appears only four times in the Bible, all in solemn and poetic passages: three times in Deuteronomy 32—33 (the song of Moses and his final blessings), once in Isaiah 44. In Deuteronomy 32:15, Moses uses it ironically: he reminds Israel of its ideal name to better show its fall into sin and idolatry. In Deuteronomy 33:26 and Isaiah 44:2, the term evokes instead the dignity of the people and God's tenderness. It is a name for important moments, when it is necessary to remind Israel who it truly is in the eyes of the Lord.
H3484.portee: This name reminds us that God sees His people not only for what they currently are, with their weaknesses, but for who they can become and who they are destined to be. To be called Yeshurun is to be called to uprightness and obedience. For the Christian, this name speaks of God's wonderful purpose: to be "upright," just, living according to His will, carried by His grace.

sens: Ninth son of Jacob, son of Leah
H3485G.detail: 1. Issachar is the ninth son of Jacob and the fifth child that Leah bore to her husband. His name means "there is a reward" or "God has given me my wages": Leah named him thus to celebrate the fact that God had regarded her work and dignity (Genesis 30:18). He is the brother of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, born of Leah, and half-brother to Joseph and Benjamin, born of Rachel.
H3485G.origine: The name Issachar comes from a Hebrew root meaning "wage" or "reward," related to the verb "to praise" or "to pay." It expresses the action of God who recognizes and rewards. Leah chose this name to thank God for having paid attention to her while she was less loved than her sister Rachel.
H3485G.emploi: Issachar primarily designates the son of Jacob, mentioned for the first time in Genesis 30:18 at his birth. He later appears in genealogies (Genesis 35:23, 46:13; 1 Chronicles 2:1) and in Jacob's final blessings (Genesis 49:14). The name also extends to the tribe of Israel descended from him: it receives territory in Canaan during the land distribution (Joshua 19:17-23) and is included in all the census of the desert (Numbers 1:28-29, 26:23-25). The tribe of Issachar is known for its wisdom and knowledge: 1 Chronicles 12:32 notably mentions it. The name also appears in prophetic contexts, such as the vision of the final distribution in Ezekiel 48.
H3485G.portee: Issachar reminds us that God recognizes and rewards faithfulness, even that of the least. His story shows how God integrates everyone into His plan, including those who feel less favored. The tribe of Issachar, renowned for its wisdom, invites believers to cultivate knowledge and understanding in the fear of God.

sens: One of the sons of the prophet Obed-Edom, gatekeeper of the temple during the time of the united Kingdom
son of Obed-Edom and brother of Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Shachar, Nethanel, Ammiel, and Peullethai
H3485H.detail: Issachar is a Levite from the tribe of Korah (descendant of a famous family of singers and temple gatekeepers). He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:5, where he is designated as the seventh son of Obed-Edom and as a temple gatekeeper — that is, guardian of the sanctuary gates, an important function entrusted to the Levites. The text notes that God had blessed him, which emphasizes that this charge was a privilege granted by divine grace. He should not be confused with the more famous Issachar, who was the ninth son of Jacob and whose descendants formed one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
H3485H.origine: The name Issachar means "there is a reward" or "reward granted" in Hebrew. It is composed of a root that evokes the idea of salary, price, or reward received. This name expresses a feeling of gratitude toward God for His blessings and favors.
H3485H.emploi: This Issachar, son of Obed-Edom, appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 26:5. He is listed among the sons of Obed-Edom who, during the time of the united Kingdom of Israel, served as temple gatekeepers in Jerusalem. This family of Levites was known to be particularly blessed by God, which earned them important responsibilities in worship. His name in the official genealogy shows that he was a recognized and trustworthy man in the administration of the sanctuary.

sens: physical sign of old age
elderly person, old man
H3486.detail:
1. The word literally refers to white hair, which naturally appears with advanced age. In 2 Chronicles 36:17, during the siege of Jerusalem, the text lists the victims without distinction: young men, young women, and those with white hair, showing that none are spared, from the youngest to the oldest.
2. By extension, the word designates the elderly person themselves, one who has white hair — the old man or old woman. It is a concrete and respectful way to speak of the elders, emphasizing the visible sign of their long life.
H3486.origine: The Hebrew word יָשֵׁשׁ (yashesh) expresses the idea of whiteness and old age. It comes from a root that evokes the loss of color and the weakening associated with age. In the Hebrew Bible, white hair is a universal sign of wisdom and seniority, but also of fragility and proximity to death.
H3486.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 36:17. It is found in the account of the last days of Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar II besieges the city. The context highlights the total horror: the Chaldean king makes no distinction between ages, indiscriminately killing young men, young women, and the elderly. The term emphasizes the extremity of human life — those who have white hair, in other words, those who have survived the longest.
H3486.portee: This verse reminds us of the terrible reality of war and judgment: no one is spared, not even the elderly who deserved respect and protection according to the Mosaic law. It raises the question of divine justice and the suffering of the innocent, inviting the believer to meditate on the weight of collective sin and the necessity of repentance.

sens: Particle that marks the direct object of an action
Grammatical element without an equivalent in French, used only in biblical Aramaic
H3487.detail: 1. In Aramaic, as in Hebrew, this grammatical particle is used before the direct object complement of the verb: it is not translated, but it signals to the reader that the word that follows receives the action of the verb. For example, in Daniel 3:12, "they accused the Jews" — the word "Jews" (in Aramaic) is preceded by this particle to show that it is the Jews who are being accused, not the other way around. 2. It is a purely grammatical tool of the Aramaic system, without inherent meaning: it does not exist in modern French or English, where word order is sufficient to indicate who does what and who suffers the action.
H3487.origine: This Aramaic particle is equivalent to the Hebrew particle אֵת (et, H0853), which served the same function in the Hebrew texts of the Old Testament. Both forms belong to the same ancient Semitic grammatical system, where marking the direct object was necessary to avoid ambiguities. In Aramaic, this particle has been preserved with the same purely functional value.
H3487.emploi: This particle appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 3:12, where it is found in an Aramaic discourse reporting the accusation against Daniel's three companions. Its use there is strictly grammatical: it helps with the syntactical clarity of the passage, as it does everywhere else in biblical Aramaic. Although unique in the available references, it follows the same pattern as the analogous Hebrew particle, which is very frequent in the Old Testament.

sens: To take or occupy a sitting position
To dwell, inhabit a place
To sit as a judge or authority
To occupy a throne or position of power
H3488.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to sit, that is, to take a place on a seat. In Daniel 7:9, the Ancient of Days "sat" on his throne, an act that marks the beginning of a solemn vision of divine judgment.
2. The word can also mean to dwell or inhabit somewhere: in Ezra 4:10 and 4:17, peoples are "established" or "dwell" in a region, meaning they are settled there durably.
3. To sit carries judicial authority: in Daniel 7:10, the judges "sat" to proceed with the judgment, and the word "judgment" in Daniel 7:26 refers to this sitting of the courts, at the moment when the verdict is pronounced.
4. The throne is the seat of power: to sit on a throne means to reign and exercise sovereign authority.
H3488.origine: The Aramaic root יתב (yetiv) expresses the idea of remaining in place, of establishing oneself. The related Hebrew verb is יֵשֵׁב (yashav), which carries the same meanings. These two verbs are connected to a fundamental image: that of immobility, of durable rest, whether physical (to sit) or territorial (to inhabit). In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, we find κάθημαι (kathêmai), "to be seated."
H3488.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only five times in the New Testament and the Old Testament as we have it. It is attested in two books: Ezra (two occurrences) and Daniel (three). In Ezra, it refers to the settling of populations in territory. In Daniel, particularly in chapters 7:9 and 7:10, it takes on a major theological dimension: the Ancient of Days sits, the judges sat for the final judgment. It is a verb of stability and authority, often linked to the great events of the divine plan.
H3488.portee: For the biblical reader, this verb reminds us that God does not remain passive in history: he sits to judge. The image of God "sitting" on his throne expresses his sovereignty, stability, and absolute authority. It invites the believer to recognize that divine judgment is certain and that history culminates in a moment of final verdict.

sens: Peg or stake driven into the ground to hold up a tent or structure
Nail driven in to fix or suspend something
Pointed instrument used in weaving
That which is stable, secure, that on which one can rely
H3489.detail:
1. A stake is primarily a pointed peg driven into the ground to hold up a tent or delineate an enclosure. The tabernacle, the holy tent, was secured to the ground by these stakes driven into the earth (Exodus 27:19; Isaiah 54:2). It is a simple yet essential object for solidity and stability.
2. The word also refers to a nail, a metal or wooden peg driven in to fix or suspend a heavy object. When speaking of a nail driven into a secure place (Isaiah 22:23), the image is that of a solid and durable fixation that is unlikely to fall.
3. In weaving, the yatéd served as a peg or point to manipulate the threads and maintain the fabric. Samson used stakes of this type when Delilah bound him with cords attached to the loom (Judges 16:13-14).
4. Figuratively, the word evokes stability, security, that which does not move and on which one can count — a solid foundation in the desert (Isaiah 33:20) or a reliable basis for trust.
H3489.origine: The Hebrew word yatéd comes from a root that means "to drive in" or "to pierce." It is a concrete, simple object that appears in many ancient Near Eastern civilizations. The family of the word includes the verb "to drive into the ground." The starting image is that of a quick and direct movement: to drive something pointed into the soil.
H3489.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Bible, concentrated mainly in the historical and prophetic books. It is first encountered in the books of Exodus and Numbers, where it refers to the stakes of the tabernacle and its enclosure — the necessary material equipment for worship in motion in the desert. The judges use it in concrete narratives: Jael drives a stake into the head of Sisera (Judges 4:21; 5:26). The prophets, notably Isaiah, use it figuratively to speak of what is solid and durable — a nail driven in securely, a well-established dwelling. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: material when it concerns the tabernacle or tents, warrior when it concerns a weapon, and spiritual when it symbolizes stability.
H3489.portee: The stake reminds the reader that the life of faith rests on solid foundations — just as the tabernacle was secured to the ground by these simple pegs, our relationship with God needs to be anchored and stable. The image of the nail driven into a secure place (Isaiah 22:23) invites us to seek in God a foundation that nothing can shake. It is a humble yet powerful image: it is not great monuments that ensure stability, but simple, well-planted, durable elements.

sens: a child whose father is dead
one who is without protection or support
a figure of weakness and vulnerability in the face of oppression
H3490.detail:
1. An orphan is literally a child who has lost their father and is deprived of the familial support that should have protected them (Exodus 22:22). In biblical culture, this loss was particularly grave as the father ensured the livelihood and defense of the entire family.
2. The word more broadly designates all those who are defenseless: orphans of fathers, but also isolated individuals, lacking protective power. Job speaks of those whose "arms are broken" (Job 22:9), meaning without strength or support.
3. The orphan becomes the biblical image of one who can easily be oppressed, robbed, or mistreated (Proverbs 23:10; Jeremiah 22:3), because they lack an intercessor. This is why God presents Himself as their defender: "The Father of the fatherless" (Psalms 68:6).
H3490.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking absence, deprivation. It is a specifically Hebrew word designating one who lacks a father, an important distinction in a patriarchal society where the father was the source of all rights and protection. The Mosaic Law regularly mentions the orphan alongside the foreigner and the widow, three figures of vulnerability that God wants His people to protect.
H3490.emploi: The word "orphan" appears 42 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets. In Deuteronomy, it is constantly associated with social duty: orphans have the right to the forgotten sheaf (24:19), to the tithe (26:12), to the feast (16:11). In the Psalms, the orphan is one whom God defends against their oppressors (10:18; 82:3), one whom the Father of mercy cares for (68:6). In the Prophets, mistreating the orphan becomes the major sign of injustice that cries out for vengeance (Jeremiah 22:3; Isaiah 1:17). Job presents wicked men who plunder orphans (24:3, 24:9). The image of the orphan gains spiritual depth: it represents every weak person in the face of sin, in need of divine protection.
H3490.portee: The orphan in the Bible is not just a social reality; it is a call from God to His people. Protecting the orphan is to imitate God Himself and recognize that no injustice escapes His eyes. This word challenges every believer regarding their duty of justice and mercy towards the most vulnerable. It also reminds us that every child of God is in some way an orphan in this world, completely dependent on the protection of the Heavenly Father.

sens: Fortified city in the mountains of Judah, in the southern territory
City assigned to the Levitical priests descended from Aaron
H3492.detail:
1. Jatthir is a city located in the mountainous region of Judah, listed among the cities of the Judean territory (Joshua 15:48). The Hebrew name means "abundance" or "rich land," likely due to the fertility of the heights where it was located.
2. The city was given to the Levitical priests, descendants of Aaron, as one of their cities of refuge (1 Chronicles 6:57; Joshua 21:14). It was one of the forty-eight cities assigned to the Levites so that they would have a place to live and minister among the people of Israel.
H3492.origine: The name Jatthir comes from the Hebrew יַתִּיר (yattîr), derived from a root meaning "abundance" or "surplus." This name reflects the perceived richness or fertility of the place. Several cities in Israel bore names evoking abundance or characteristics of the terrain, revealing how the ancient Israelites named their settlements after natural resources.
H3492.emploi: Jatthir appears four times in the Bible. It first appears in the list of cities in the mountains of Judah (Joshua 15:48), which enumerates the strongholds of the southern territory. It is then mentioned among the Levitical cities given to the sons of Aaron (Joshua 21:14 and 1 Chronicles 6:57), confirming its status as a priestly city. Finally, it is cited in the account where David sends gifts to the elders of Judah after his victory over the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30:27), showing that the city was a recognized population center where David sought the support of the people.

sens: That exceeds ordinary measure, remarkable in size or quality
Surpassing others in power, ability, excellence
Carried to an excessive, extreme degree
Of unusual intensity or force
H3493.detail:
1. The word describes what is out of the ordinary by its size, splendor, or appearance. The great statue that King Nebuchadnezzar sees in a dream is of "extraordinary" splendor (Daniel 2:31), striking the imagination with its majestic and impressive appearance.
2. It qualifies a personal excellence or superiority, particularly in wisdom and ability. Daniel possesses a "superior spirit" (Daniel 5:12), meaning an intelligence and understanding that surpass those of his peers, making him capable of solving enigmas that others cannot.
3. It expresses the intensity or extreme degree of a reality. When the furnace is heated "extraordinarily," the order is severe and the heat pushed to an excessive point (Daniel 3:22).
4. It reinforces the idea of royal power and dominance, as when Nebuchadnezzar's power "only increased" (Daniel 4:36), marking an unmatched strength.
H3493.origine: The Hebrew word יַתִּיר comes from a root meaning "to exceed, surpass." It fundamentally expresses the idea of what goes beyond the common, the normal limit. This root also appears in the verb יתר ("to remain in excess, to be too much"). The word belongs to the vocabulary of late Hebrew Bible, particularly in the book of Daniel, where it serves to magnify the realities of the Persian world and divine visions.
H3493.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the book of Daniel, which describes the experiences of the prophet in Babylon. It is used to qualify impressive material realities (the immense statue, the overheated furnace) as well as spiritual or moral qualities (Daniel's superior spirit, his extraordinary wisdom). Its uses oscillate between the adjective ("extraordinary," "superior") and the adverb ("extraordinarily"), depending on the sentence structure. In the context of Daniel, the word constantly emphasizes how the prophet and his faith surpass the Persian world, and how God manifests His power in visibly exceptional ways.
H3493.portee: This word reminds the reader that God often acts in ways that exceed the ordinary and impress even the powerful of the world. Daniel's "extraordinary wisdom" illustrates how authentic faith and obedience to God confer an excellence that no human power can match. Recognizing the extraordinary nature of divine action invites the believer to see beyond appearances and trust in the superiority of divine wisdom over that of the world.

sens: City in the territory of the tribe of Dan in southern Canaan
H3494.detail: Jithla is a city that is part of the inheritance assigned to the tribe of Dan during the division of the promised land. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:42, in the list of cities that God gave to this tribe. Its name literally means "the one who hangs" or "it hangs," likely a geographical reference or to a forgotten local event.
H3494.origine: The Hebrew name yit.lah comes from a root evoking the action of hanging or suspending. This type of geographical name was common in Canaan, often forged from a memorable event or a characteristic of the place. The name reflects how the peoples of this region named their cities according to concrete images.
H3494.emploi: Jithla appears only once in the biblical accounts, in Joshua 19:42, in the midst of the enumeration of the cities in the southern territory of Dan. It is cited alongside Shaalabbin and Ajalon, all three located in the same region. This unique mention makes it a minor city in the biblical narrative, but it shows how God had precisely distributed the territory to each of the tribes of Israel.

sens: Moabite warrior in the service of King David
H3495.detail: Jithma is a Moabite soldier who was among David's renowned warriors. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of the 'Mighty Men' of the king (1 Chronicles 11:46), which shows that he had gained a distinguished military reputation despite his foreign origins.
H3495.origine: The name Jithma means 'orphan' in Hebrew. Nothing is known about his circumstances of birth, but his name suggests that he may have grown up without parents — which makes his military career all the more remarkable.
H3495.emploi: Jithma appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:46, where he is listed among the warriors who made up David's elite military. This brief appearance shows that men from various backgrounds, including foreigners like this Moabite, could attain the highest military positions under David's reign, recognized for their bravery and loyalty.
H3495.portee: Jithma illustrates how God recognizes courage and faithfulness beyond national and social barriers. His story, though short, reminds us that humble origins or the status of being a foreigner do not limit what God can accomplish through a life dedicated to faithful service.

sens: Son of Meshlemiah, one of the temple gatekeepers
Levite from the Korahite family
Fourth son of Meshlemiah
H3496.detail:
1. Jathniel is a man living during the time of the Divided Monarchy (see 1 Chronicles 26:2). He is the son of Meshlemiah, one of the gatekeepers of the temple in Jerusalem.
2. Jathniel belongs to the Korahite family, a branch of the Levites dedicated to the service of worship. This lineage of Levites was specially tasked with important functions in the temple.
3. In the list of his brothers given in 1 Chronicles 26:2, Jathniel is named as the fourth son of Meshlemiah, after Zechariah, Jediah, and Zebadiah.
H3496.origine: The name Jathniel means 'God praises' or 'God has praised me'. It is composed of the Hebrew verb that expresses praise and the divine name El (God). This name expresses recognition towards God for His blessings or acts of thanksgiving.
H3496.emploi: Jathniel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:2. He appears in the genealogy of Meshlemiah, where the sons who served as gatekeepers at the temple are listed. No specific details about his life or ministry are provided; he is simply identified as one of the descendants of the Korahite priestly family.

sens: City in the southern region of Judah
H3497.detail: Ithnan is a city in the extreme south of Judah, listed among the localities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised lands. It appears only once in the Bible, in the list of southern Judean cities (Joshua 15:23).
H3497.origine: The name Ithnan literally means 'wage' or 'rent' in ancient Hebrew, likely related to the idea of reward or compensation. Its etymology remains obscure, but it reflects how ancient place names often mirrored concepts or values of daily life.
H3497.emploi: Ithnan is mentioned only once in Scripture, in chapter 15 of the book of Joshua. It is included in the enumeration of cities in the Negev (the southern desert) assigned to the tribe of Judah during the conquest and division of Canaan. Its presence in this list indicates that it was a real settlement, located in the arid lands of southern Judah, although it is of little importance in the biblical narrative. Its exact location is not identified with certainty.

sens: What remains after a part has been removed or consumed
To survive, not to be destroyed or annihilated
To be in excess, to exceed the normal measure
To keep, to set aside for later
To surpass, to excel over others
To persist over time or in a state
H3498.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a material remainder: after something has been taken or eaten, a part remains. In Exodus 12:10, the Israelites are not to let any of the Passover lamb remain until morning — this refers to what physically subsists. In Genesis 30:36, Jacob lets the remainder of Laban's flock graze, meaning the portion that remains after separation.
2. The word also expresses survival, the fact of not being annihilated. When David fears that Absalom has killed all his sons, he says that not one has remained (2 Samuel 13:30): no one has survived. Isaiah 1:9 speaks of 'a few survivors' after devastation — those who remain alive.
3. To have in excess or abundance: Deuteronomy 28:11 promises that the Lord will give an abundance of well-being. This conveys the idea of surplus, having more than necessary.
4. To reserve for future use, to keep. Leviticus 7:16-17 prescribes that the leftovers from thank offerings must be eaten the next day, implying that they should be kept.
5. To excel, to surpass: Genesis 49:4 tells Reuben 'You shall not excel' — the verb here means to exceed others, to have the first place.
6. To persist, to remain in a state or condition — not just a one-time action, but a continuity. Leviticus 10:16 speaks of the sons who remained with Aaron, meaning who stayed with him.
H3498.origine: The verb yatar comes from a root that expresses the idea of 'what remains' or 'what exceeds'. Related to notions of abundance and surplus, it evokes the image of overflow — what exceeds or overflows the necessary. In Hebrew, the noun 'yeter' denotes the surplus, the supplement. The underlying image is that of exceeding: something that goes beyond the expected limit, whether in quantity (something remains) or in excellence (it surpasses).
H3498.emploi: The verb yatar appears about 100 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Niphal (passive form) and Hiphil (causative form). It is very frequent in the laws of Leviticus concerning sacrifices and food leftovers. In the Pentateuch and the history of Israel (Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Samuel, Kings), it serves to describe the survivors of wars or the remaining portions of a group. Isaiah notably uses it for the theological concept of 'the remnant of Israel', a remnant that God preserves. The pragmatic senses (food leftovers, remnants of peoples) largely dominate, but the prophetic context gives it a spiritual significance: the remnant is the people that God saves in judgment.
H3498.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on what God preserves amid judgment and destruction. The 'remnant' is never due to chance, but to God's faithfulness: He keeps a people for Himself. For the Christian, this speaks of spiritual survival, of what remains when the temporal collapses. It is also a call not to waste, to respect what God provides — neither before nor after, but in just measure.

sens: What remains after a part has been removed, taken, or consumed
The others, those who are not counted or designated in the first rank
What persists, what continues to exist
The excess, the surplus, the abundance
Superiority, excellence, preeminence
H3499A.detail:
1. What remains after a part has been removed: when something is divided, there is a part taken and a part that "remains." In Exodus 10:5, the fourth plague of Egypt leaves as a "remnant" what the previous locusts did not consume. In 2 Kings 25:11, the Babylonian authorities leave "the remnant of the people" in the land, those who were not deported.
2. The others, those who are not in the first rank or not specifically designated: when listing leaders, we speak of the "remnant" of the soldiers (2 Samuel 10:10). In 1 Kings 22:39, the chronicler lists the major deeds of King Ahab and then refers to the complete history: "the rest of his actions."
3. What persists or continues to exist: this conveys the idea of the survivor, of one who continues to exist. This nuance often aligns with that of remnants or leftovers, which prolong the life of something past.
4. The excess or surplus: when there is abundance, it is the "remnant" after consumption or distribution. Job 22:20 speaks of "riches" (literally: the surplus, the excess) consumed by fire.
5. Superiority, excellence, what excels or prevails: Genesis 49:3 plays on this double meaning: Reuben was "superior" in dignity and power, meaning he had a prominent rank, a preeminence among his brothers.
H3499A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to leave" or "to exceed." Its basic image is that of what remains when a part is removed — but also what exceeds, what excels. The same root provides the verb "to leave," "to abandon." The central idea is that of separation: what remains on one side while something is taken away from the other. This is why this word can refer to both the ordinary "remnant" and the "excellence": the excess is what "exceeds" the common measure.
H3499A.emploi: This word appears 90 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical books (1-2 Kings, 2 Chronicles) and in the accounts of Moses. Its most frequent usage (about 73 occurrences) is in the sense of "remnant," particularly in stereotypical phrases: "The rest of the king's actions..." (1 Kings 22:39 and passim). This phrase, which recurs dozens of times, directs readers to the royal archives for everything not recounted in the sacred text. In military or administrative contexts, it refers to the "remnant of the people" or troops, those who are not in the forefront (2 Samuel 10:10; 2 Kings 25:11). Three times, it takes on the meaning of "to leave," a direct verb closely linked to its root. The word can also mean "wealth" or "abundance" (Job 22:20; Psalms 17:14), the material surplus. Finally, in Genesis 49:3, it carries the high meaning of "superiority" or "excellence," designating a preeminence or particular dignity.
H3499A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals how the Bible allocates attention: what deserves to be told in detail is separated from the "remnant." This view of the remnant invites us to recognize that God chooses what He wants to illuminate, and that the absence of text is not an absence of meaning. Spiritually, the "remnant" gains a deep resonance in the Old Testament, heralding the remnants of Israel that endure and in whom God fulfills His promises. Understanding this word is learning to read the Bible according to its priorities.

sens: Braided or twisted link used to tie, hold, or pull
String or cable of a bow intended to launch the arrow
Image of life or existence, like a thread that can be cut
H3499B.detail:
1. A cord is a link made of braided or twisted material — like those with which the Philistines tried to bind Samson (Judges 16:7-9). Samson claims that with simple fresh cords he would become weak, but when the enemies use them to capture him, he tears them apart like a burning tow cord: the cord is the quintessential physical link, malleable yet also breakable.
2. The cord is also the string of the bow that propels the arrow: in Psalm 11:2, the wicked "adjust their arrow on the cord" to shoot their dart. Here it is the driving element of a weapon, taut and releasable.
3. Metaphorically, life itself is compared to a cord that can be "cut" (Job 4:21): an image to speak of death or the end of existence. Similarly, the "restraint" or brake that Job's adversaries abandon (Job 30:11) is also expressed by this word, as if the cord that held back their behavior had snapped.
H3499B.origine: The Hebrew word יֶתֶר (yeter) comes from a root that suggests the idea of remaining, subsisting, or extending. It primarily denotes anything that is stretched or extended — a cord, a link — because these objects maintain this characteristic tension. The basic image is that of something flexible yet firm, capable of binding or projecting. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of ancient daily life: cords for wells, tents, weapons, all essential objects.
H3499B.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible. Three occurrences concern the cords with which they attempted to bind Samson (Judges 16:7-9), the key moment when his superhuman strength is manifested by the breaking of these material ties. A metaphorical occurrence is found in Job 4:21, where a person's life is compared to a cord that is cut — a poetic way of speaking about death. In Job 30:11, the word evokes rather a restraint or moral brake: the absence of a cord signifies the absence of control. Finally, in Psalm 11:2, the bowstring is the technical element by which the archer shoots. Each context reminds us that the cord is a link, either literal or figurative — something that holds, activates, or can be broken.
H3499B.portee: The cord embodies both fragility and strength: it may seem insignificant, but it can also bind, project, or save a life. For the believer, it reminds us that life itself hangs by a thread — a thread that God can cut at His appointed time — and that no human link can truly hold back one whom God has marked with His hand. In the story of Samson, the cord becomes a symbol of human constraints, powerless against the strength that God gives to His chosen one.
